Contribution of diazotrophy to nitrogen inputs supporting Karenia brevis blooms in the Gulf of Mexico M.R. Mulholland a,*, P.W. Bernhardt a, I. Ozmon a, L.A. Procise a, M. Garrett b, J.M. O’Neil c, C.A. Heil b,1, D.A. Bronk d a Department of Ocean, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, Old Dominion University, 4600 Elkhorn Avenue, Norfolk, VA 23529, USA b Fish and Wildlife Research Institute, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, St. Petersburg, FL, USA c Horn Point Laboratory, University of Maryland, Cambridge, MD 21613, USA d Department of Physical Sciences, The College of William & Mary, Virginia Institute of Marine Science, Gloucester Point, VA 23062, USA A B S T R A C T Blooms of Karenia brevis plague the West Florida Shelf (WFS) region in the Gulf of Mexico (GOM) where they exert harmful effects on aquatic biota and humans. Because productivity on the WFS is N limited, new N inputs into the region are thought to trigger blooms of K. brevis. Here we examine the potential for new N inputs via N2 fixation by Trichodesmium and other diazotrophic plankton to contribute to the N demand of K. brevis. Because of possible methodological biases, we also compared N2 fixation rates by cultured Trichodesmium using the 15N2 bubble addition method and the 15N2 saturated seawater. Both methods yielded identical results in 12 and 24 h incubations; however, there was more variability in rate estimates made using the bubble addition method. Pelagic N2 fixation rates by other planktonic diazotrophs ranged from 0 to 13.6 nmol N L−1 d−1, comparable to or higher than rates observed in oligotrophic gyres. These rates should be considered conservative estimates because they were made using the bubble addition method. Integrating over our study area, we estimate that new inputs of N to the WFS via N2 fixation are on the order of 0.011 Tmol N annually. Further, we measured directly the trophic transfer of recently fixed N2 to co-occurring plankton that included K. brevis and found that up to 47% of N2 fixed was transferred to non-diazotrophic plankton even in short (<6 h) incubations where N2 fixation was likely underestimated. © 2014 Elsevier B.V. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction Blooms of the red tide dinoflagellate, Karenia brevis, have devastating impacts on the local and regional economies in the Gulf of Mexico, including those adjacent to the West Florida Shelf (WFS). Despite years of targeted programs aimed at prediction and mitigation of blooms, massive blooms continue to occur, are not well forecast, and exert devastating impacts when and where they occur. Because many harmful algal blooms are attributed directly or indirectly to cultural eutrophication (Heisler et al., 2008), major research campaigns have been undertaken to determine whether anthropogenic nutrient inputs fuel or enhance red tides. Studies quantifying natural and anthropogenic nutrient inputs to the WFS region and relating them to the occurrence of red tides there suggest an N deficit (Vargo et al., 2004). Models, anecdotal observations, and recent measurements of N2 fixation by Trichodesmium suggest that natural inputs of new nitrogen (N) via dinitrogen (N2) fixation might provide the “missing” N necessary to support blooms on the WFS (Walsh and Steidinger, 2001; Mulholland et al., 2006; Lenes and Heil, 2010). Further, the direct transfer of recently fixed N2 to co-occurring phytoplankton, including Karenia brevis, was observed in one small study (Mulholland et al., 2004a,b). Here, we expand upon previous studies examining N2 fixation by Trichodesmium (Mulholland et al., 2006) and the trophic transfer of recently fixed N from Trichodesmium to co-occurring plankton (Mulholland et al., 2004a,b), and also estimate rates of pelagic N2 fixation concurrent with the development and persistence of Karenia brevis populations. Because it has been projected that N2 fixation will increase in response to elevated pCO2 and climate forcing (Hutchins et al., 2007, 2009; Levitan et al., 2007; Barcelos e Ramos et al., 2007), determining the present relationship between diazotrophic N inputs and productivity of planktonic food webs that include harmful algae is crucial for projecting the likelihood of blooms in the future. 2. Methods We measured: (1) N2 fixation by Trichodesmium (Mulholland et al., 2006), (2) N2 fixation by pelagic diazotrophs, and (3) the trophic transfer of recently fixed N2 from Trichodesmium to co-occurring plankton during incubation experiments (Mulholland et al., 2004a,b) during cruise transects on the WFS. Trichodesmium abundance has been shown to be highest between June and September (Lenes and Heil, 2010). Therefore from 2001 to 2003, we conducted two cruises per year, one in summer when Trichodesmium are known to be abundant, and one in fall when Karenia brevis blooms are frequently observed. In 2001, cruises were aboard the R/V Walton Smith (July) and the R/V Suncoaster (October); in 2002, cruises were aboard the R/V Walton Smith (July and October); in 2003 cruises were aboard the R/V Pelican (June and November). Additional details for cruises between 2001 and 2003 can be found in Mulholland et al. (2006). Between 2006 and 2010, cruises were conducted only during October when K. brevis is usually present and can be abundant but Trichodesmium is not. During 2006, the cruise was aboard the R/V Suncoaster while cruises in 2007, 2008, 2009, and 2010 were aboard the R/V Pelican. Stations sampled during cruises are shown in Fig. 1. During all cruises, samples were collected for analysis of chlorophyll a (Chl a). These samples were filtered onto glass fiber (Whatman GF/F) filters (0.7 μm pore size) and frozen in sterile centrifuge tubes and analyzed within 2 weeks of sample collection (Welschmeyer, 1994). Rate estimates for N_2 fixation by Trichodesmium colonies were reported previously from cruises undertaken from 2001 to 2003 (Mulholland et al., 2006) and are summarized in Table 1. For Trichodesmium, rates of N_2 fixation were estimated using the acetylene reduction method (Capone, 1993) and using ^{15}N_2 (Montoya et al., 1996; Mulholland et al., 2004a,b, see below). Acetylene (C_2H_2) reduction assays were initiated by removing 2 mL of headspace from 24 mL serum vials containing 10 mL of 0.2 μm filtered seawater and 10 colonies of Trichodesmium and then adding 2 mL of C_2H_2. Immediately after the C_2H_2 addition, and at increments over the course of the day, 100 μL of headspace was removed and the production of ethylene was measured using a Shimadzu gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector. To calculate N_2 fixation from C_2H_2 reduction, we used a 3:1 conversion factor. Uptake experiments using the ^{15}N_2 bubble addition method were initiated by adding tracer additions (<10%) of highly enriched (99%) ^{15}N_2 to gas tight bottles (315 or 727 mL) filled with whole water or <0.2 μm filtered seawater containing 50 or 100 colonies of Trichodesmium (Mulholland and Capone, 2001). Incubation bottles were placed in on-deck incubators equipped with flow-through seawater to maintain near-ambient temperatures. Because the ^{15}N_2 bubble doesn't equilibrate immediately (Mohr et al., 2010; Großkopf et al., 2012), the atom% enrichment was likely less than 10% over most of the incubation period. This would cause an underestimate of N_2 fixation rates using the mixing model (Montoya et al., 1996; Orcutt et al., 2001) if the atom% enrichment of the dissolved N_2 pool was actually lower than that assumed based on instantaneous equilibration of the gas addition (Mulholland et al., 2012). After 12 or 24 h, incubations were terminated by filtration through pre-combusted (450 °C for 2 h) Whatman glass fiber (GF/F) filters. Samples were frozen in sterile cryotubes until analysis. In addition to estimating N_2 fixation by Trichodesmium, we measured the trophic transfer of recently fixed N_2, during cruises in 2001 and 2002 (see also Mulholland et al., 2004a,b). To do this, we placed Trichodesmium colonies in 0.2 μm filtered seawater and then poured them into dialysis tubing with either 1 kilo-Dalton (kD) or 100 kD size cut-offs. We then sealed the tubes and suspended them in gas-tight bottles containing natural whole water samples of plankton communities (see also Mulholland et al., 2004a,b). In addition we prepared control incubations containing whole seawater without added Trichodesmium. During three of the trophic transfer experiments, we also added copepods (Macrosetella gracilis) that are known to graze on Trichodesmium (O'Neil and Roman, 1994) to the dialysis bags to determine whether grazer-mediated processes enhanced the trophic transfer of N_2 fixed by diazotrophs. During two of the experiments we added viruses concentrated from natural seawater samples via ultrafiltration to the dialysis bags to determine whether viruses would enhance the transfer of fixed N from Trichodesmium to co-occurring plankton.

Stations were occupied inside and outside of Tampa Bay (TB) and Charlotte Harbor (CH), and seaward of Sarasota Bay (SB) and the Caloosahatchee River (CR). To initiate trophic transfer experiments, we added \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) gas, as described above (bubble method) which we recognize underestimates N\(_2\) fixation. After 6–8 h, we terminated incubations by filtering their contents. For control bottles, the entire contents were gently through pre-combusted Whatman GF/F filters. For bottles containing dialysis bags filled with *Trichodesmium*, we removed the dialysis tubing and filtered its contents through pre-combusted Whatman GF/F filters to measure the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}\) enrichment of *Trichodesmium*, we then filtered the whole water from the incubation bottle onto a separate pre-combusted GF/F filter to measure its enrichment. For experiments with added copepods, at the end of the incubation period, the copepods were separated from the *Trichodesmium* and collected onto an additional set of pre-combusted GF/F filters. All filters were stored frozen in sterile cryotubes until analysis. Annual cruises conducted between 2006 and 2010 targeted the period when *Karenia brevis* blooms often initiate (October) but when *Trichodesmium* are not abundant on the WFS. Consequently, *Trichodesmium* were not sampled during cruises between 2006 and 2010. During these cruises we measured rates of pelagic N\(_2\) fixation in natural seawater samples for comparison to *Trichodesmium*-specific N\(_2\) fixation rates on the WFS. Water samples were collected from near the surface (upper 6 m) and at the fluorescence maximum using Niskin bottles mounted to a sampling rosette equipped with a conductivity, temperature, and depth (CTD) sensor. Whole water was transferred directly to gas-tight incubation bottles for uptake experiments using the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) bubble addition method (Montoya et al., 1996). Uptake experiments were initiated by adding tracer additions (<10%) of highly enriched (99%) \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) to gas-tight bottles filled with whole water collected from near the surface or at the fluorescence maximum (Montoya et al., 1996; Mulholland et al., 2006). We recognize that this method may underestimate N\(_2\) fixation, because the \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) gas addition takes time to equilibrate with the seawater (Mohr et al., 2010); estimates suggest that this method underestimates N\(_2\) fixation by a factor of 1.4 to 2 although direct comparisons suggest this is highly variable (Großkopf et al., 2012; Mulholland et al., 2012). To estimate the potential bias of using the bubble method (Montoya et al., 1996), we conducted a small laboratory experiment using *Trichodesmium* isolate IMS101 growing on YBCII medium under a 12:12 L:D cycle as described previously (Mulholland and Bernhardt, 2005). We conducted paired comparisons wherein we estimated N\(_2\) fixation rates using the bubble method and \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) equilibrated seawater in cultures of *Trichodesmium* incubated for 12 and 24 h. We placed culture aliquots in 12 pre-combusted glass incubation bottles. Six of the incubation bottles received bubble additions calculated to be a 10% enrichment of the dissolved N\(_2\) pool. The other six bottles were amended with a 10% addition of \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\)-saturated seawater prepared as described by Mohr et al. (2010). Triplicate bottles from bubble and saturated-seawater \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) amendments were sacrificed after 12 and 24 h. There were no differences in calculated \(^{15}\mathrm{N}_2\) uptake rates between the treatments regardless of the incubation length (Fig. 2). Frozen samples were dried, pelletized into tin disks, and analyzed for total particulate N (PN) and carbon (PC) and isotopic enrichment on a Europa isotope ratio mass spectrometer equipped with an automated nitrogen and carbon analyzer (ANCA) preparation module. However, because we accounted for the changing isotopic enrichment of *Trichodesmium* over the course of incubations and incorporated this variable enrichment into our uptake calculation for co-occurring plankton, our estimates of the percent of recently fixed N_2 that was transferred to co-occurring plankton are not biased in the same way as our estimates of N_2 fixation rates using the bubble addition method because we accounted only for ^15N atoms that were fixed and then recovered in co-occurring plankton. We used an exponential average to estimate the changing enrichment of *Trichodesmium* over the course of incubations, thus our estimates of the trophic transfer of N could be biased if enrichment of *Trichodesmium* deviated from this model. Areal rates of N_2 fixation were calculated by pooling and then averaging our pelagic rate measurements from the surface mixed layer and fluorescence maximum and accounting for seasonal N_2 fixation by *Trichodesmium* (Mulholland et al., 2006). We then calculated depth-integrated N_2 fixation rates estimates over an average euphotic depth of 20 m. We calculated areal N_2 fixation rates over the shelf area between Naples and Cedar Key extending to the 40 m isobath, an area of about 2.33 × 10^4 km^2 (Vargo et al., 1987). For *Trichodesmium*, we calculated new N inputs based on an average colony density of 20 col L^{-1} between June and September (Lenes and Heil, 2010). For other pelagic diazotrophs, we assumed that N_2 fixation occurred year-round. We did not include N_2 fixation by the mat-forming diazotroph *Lyngbya* sp. in this calculation, although it is known to fix N_2 in the study area, because we do not have quantitative abundance data for this cyanobacteria (see Ozmon et al., this volume). 3. Results We previously ascertained that N_2 fixation rates by *Trichodesmium* collected on the WFS during cruises from 2001 to 2003, were on average 8.79 nmol N col^{-1} d^{-1} (range of 3.3 to 20.5 nmol N col^{-1} d^{-1}) using the acetylene reduction method and 4.61 nmol N col^{-1} d^{-1} (range of 2.06 to 9.21 nmol N col^{-1} d^{-1}) – 1) using the ^15N_2 uptake method (Table 1). Our trophic transfer experiments indicated that even during short incubations (<6 h), when the bubble method can underestimate N₂ fixation (Mohr et al., 2010), that up to 47.6% of recently fixed N₂ was transferred to co-occurring plankton. Results were variable between incubation bottles (Fig. 3). The transfer of recently fixed N₂ to surrounding plankton was greater in treatments where Trichodesmium was contained in the higher molecular weight cut-off (100 kD) dialysis tubing than in treatments using the lower molecular weight cut-off (1 kD) dialysis tubing. This suggests that release of the larger dissolved organic N (DON) compounds, rather than NH₄⁺ or free amino acids were used preferentially by co-occurring taxa. Pelagic N₂ fixation rates measured during short-term (~6 h) incubation experiments (control incubations for trophic transfer experiments) on cruises between 2001 and 2003 ranged from 0.13 to 2.80 nmol N L⁻¹ d⁻¹. When pelagic N₂ fixation rates were measured in a systematic fashion during both 12 and 24 h incubation experiments between 2006 and 2010 (Table 2), N₂ fixation rates ranged from the limit of analytical detection (ND) to 13.6 nmol N L⁻¹ d⁻¹ on the WFS. These are likely underestimates because of the slow equilibration time of the added \(^{15}\)N₂ gas. Integrating an average pelagic N₂ fixation rate of 6 nmol L⁻¹ d⁻¹ over the area of the WFS from Cedar Key to Naples and out to the 40 m isobath, an area of about \(2.33 \times 10^4\) km² (Vargo et al., 1987), and assuming an average euphotic depth of 20 m, we calculate that pelagic N₂ fixation contributes about 0.001 Tmol of N annually (range of 0–0.0023 Tmol yr⁻¹) to the region. For comparison, using an average Trichodesmium abundance of 20 col L⁻¹ and assuming that they fix N₂ at an average rate of 8.8 nmol N col⁻¹ d⁻¹ between June and September (a period of 122 days) over the same area, we calculate an annual input of 0.01 Tmol N to the region via N₂ fixation by Trichodesmium. 4. Discussion Trichodesmium are abundant seasonally along the WFS (Walsh and Steidinger, 2001; Lenes and Heil, 2010) where they fix N₂ at high rates (Table 1; Mulholland et al., 2006). Results presented here suggest that Trichodesmium contribute new N that fuels the growth of co-occurring plankton, including populations of Karenia brevis. In addition, we show that viruses and grazers can accelerate the transfer of recently fixed N to co-occurring plankton, thereby stimulating system productivity (Fig. 3). The N transferred from Trichodesmium to other plankton included high and low molecular weight compounds up to 100 kD in size and the transfer of N was greater when compounds larger than 1 kD were included. Trichodesmium were previously shown to release low molecular weight DON, including amino acids (Capone et al., 1994; Gilbert and Bronk, 1994), and ammonium (Mulholland et al., 2004a,b). Our results suggest that high molecular weight compounds are also rapidly transferred to co-occurring plankton. While here we calculate that up to 47.6% of recently fixed N₂ was rapidly transferred to co-occurring non-diazotrophic populations within the community, the magnitude of the N release is likely an underestimate. This is because N₂ fixation by Trichodesmium contained in dialysis bags within the incubation bottles was probably underestimated because of the slow equilibration of the \(^{15}\)N₂ bubble addition during our short incubations (Mohr et al., 2010; Großkopf et al., 2012). Although we demonstrated that in 12 and 24 h laboratory incubation experiments using cultured Trichodesmium isolates, that this problem is negligible (Fig. 1), our field experiments were of shorter duration than this (<6 h) and so likely underestimated both rates of N₂ fixation rates and the rates of trophic transfer of recently fixed N₂. However, even though the magnitude of N transferred from Trichodesmium to co-occurring plankton was likely underestimated, the percent of the labeled N transferred from diazotrophic to non-diazotrophic plankton may be accurate. That is because rates of trophic transfer of fixed N were calculated using Trichodesmium as the source pool that was enriched. As such, we used an exponential function to describe the average enrichment of Trichodesmium over time in the incubation and this was measured directly for each experiment (see Eqs. (2) and (3) above). To calculate the percent of N that was transferred then, we accounted only for \(^{15}\)N that was actually incorporated into co-occurring plankton or Trichodesmium. We determined that in addition to Trichodesmium, pelagic N₂ fixation by diazotrophic picoplankton is a significant source of new N to the WFS ecosystem (Table 2). Rates of pelagic N₂ fixation on the WFS were similar to those observed for coastal waters along the North Atlantic continental shelf between Cape Hatteras and the Georges Bank (Mulholland et al., 2012), in the English Channel (Rees et al., 2009), and the western tropical N Atlantic (Subramaniam et al., 2008), as well as oligotrophic oceanic regions elsewhere (see Table 3). In addition, the mat-forming N₂ fixer, Lyngbya majuscula, is known to bloom along the WFS (Paerl et al., 2008) and can float on the surface or attached to mangrove propagules and be advected from coastal waters to offshore regions of the WFS; L. majuscula was observed but not quantified during our cruises (Ozmon et al. unpublished data). Cyanobacterial endosymbionts were also observed at some stations during 2006. While we do not know whether these cyanobacteria were fixing N₂ along the WFS, diazotrophic endosymbionts have been observed in coastal river plumes in the western tropical N Atlantic Ocean (Foster et al., 2007; Subramaniam et al., 2008) and the western coastal N Atlantic Ocean (Mulholland et al., 2012). The diazotrophic unicellular group A cyanobacteria (UCYN-A) are also abundant in a variety of systems including N Atlantic coastal waters (Rees et al., 2009; Moisander et al., 2010; Mulholland et al., 2012) and are also likely to be present on the WFS. However, the abundance and activity of pelagic diazotrophic groups were not quantified as part of this study. Based on our calculations above, we estimate that on average, about 0.011 Tmol N yr⁻¹ is introduced annually to the WFS ecosystem through N₂ fixation by Trichodesmium and other pelagic N₂ fixers. This is about half of that estimated recently calculated for the western N Atlantic continental shelf region between 35 and 45°N (0.02 Tmol N yr⁻¹; Mulholland et al., 2012), a substantially larger area (\(3.6 \times 10^5\) km²). These estimates of new N inputs from N₂ fixation should be considered conservative estimates because of the methodological biases of the \(^{15}\)N₂ bubble method outlined above (Mohr et al., 2010; Großkopf et al., 2012). To put these estimates into context, it was previously estimated that the N demand of a moderately sized Karenia brevis bloom (\(3 \times 10^5\) cells L⁻¹) was 56–267 nmol N L⁻¹ d⁻¹ (Vargo et al., 2004). Integrating this demand over the same volume of the WFS as we did for N₂ fixation, this would represent an N requirement of 2.6–12.4 × 10⁻⁵ Tmol d⁻¹ for a moderately sized K. brevis bloom. Thus, based on our conservative estimate of the annual N inputs from N₂ fixation, we calculate that N₂ fixation could hypothetically sustain a moderately sized bloom for 89 to 423 days on the WFS. The results presented here suggest that N₂ fixation contributes new N that can potentially fuel Karenia brevis blooms along the WFS. While Trichodesmium blooms have been linked to K. brevis blooms previously (Walsh and Steidinger, 2001; Mulholland et al., 2006), pelagic N₂ fixation also contributes N to the WFS ecosystem. It has been projected that N₂ fixation will increase in the future as a result of climate change because higher temperatures and pCO₂ enhance cyanobacterial N₂ fixation (Hutchins et al., 2007, 2009; Levitan et al., 2007; Barcelos e Ramos et al., 2007). Contribution of diazotrophy to nitrogen inputs supporting Karenia brevis blooms in the Gulf of Mexico

M.R. Mulholland a,*, P.W. Bernhardt a, I. Ozmon a, L.A. Procise a, M. Garrett b, J.M. O’Neil c, C.A. Heil b,1, D.A. Bronk d

a Department of Ocean, Earth, and Atmospheric Sciences, Old Dominion University, 4600 Elkhorn Avenue, Norfolk, VA 23529, USA
b Fish and Wildlife Research Institute, Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission, St. Petersburg, FL, USA
c Horn Point Laboratory, University of Maryland, Cambridge, MD 21613, USA
d Department of Physical Sciences, The College of William & Mary, Virginia Institute of Marine Science, Gloucester Point, VA 23062, USA

A B S T R A C T

Blooms of Karenia brevis plague the West Florida Shelf (WFS) region in the Gulf of Mexico (GOM) where they exert harmful effects on aquatic biota and humans. Because productivity on the WFS is N limited, new N inputs into the region are thought to trigger blooms of K. brevis. Here we examine the potential for new N inputs via N2 fixation by Trichodesmium and other diazotrophic plankton to contribute to the N demand of K. brevis. Because of possible methodological biases, we also compared N2 fixation rates by cultured Trichodesmium using the 15N2 bubble addition method and the 15N2 saturated seawater. Both methods yielded identical results in 12 and 24 h incubations; however, there was more variability in rate estimates made using the bubble addition method. Pelagic N2 fixation rates by other planktonic diazotrophs ranged from 0 to 13.6 nmol N L−1 d−1, comparable to or higher than rates observed in oligotrophic gyres. These rates should be considered conservative estimates because they were made using the bubble addition method. Integrating over our study area, we estimate that new inputs of N to the WFS via N2 fixation are on the order of 0.011 Tmol N annually. Further, we measured directly the trophic transfer of recently fixed N2 to co-occurring plankton that included K. brevis and found that up to 47% of N2 fixed was transferred to non-diazotrophic plankton even in short (<6 h) incubations where N2 fixation was likely underestimated.

1. Introduction

Blooms of the red tide dinoflagellate, Karenia brevis, have devastating impacts on the local and regional economies in the Gulf of Mexico, including those adjacent to the West Florida Shelf (WFS). Despite years of targeted programs aimed at prediction and mitigation of blooms, massive blooms continue to occur, are not well forecast, and exert devastating impacts when and where they occur.

Because many harmful algal blooms are attributed directly or indirectly to cultural eutrophication (Heisler et al., 2008), major research campaigns have been undertaken to determine whether anthropogenic nutrient inputs fuel or enhance red tides. Studies quantifying natural and anthropogenic nutrient inputs to the WFS region and relating them to the occurrence of red tides there suggest an N deficit (Vargo et al., 2004). Models, anecdotal observations, and recent measurements of N2 fixation by Trichodesmium suggest that natural inputs of new nitrogen (N) via dinitrogen (N2) fixation might provide the “missing” N necessary to support blooms on the WFS (Walsh and Steidinger, 2001; Mulholland et al., 2006; Lenes and Heil, 2010). Further, the direct transfer of recently fixed N2 to co-occurring phytoplankton, including Karenia brevis, was observed in one small study (Mulholland et al., 2004a,b).

Here, we expand upon previous studies examining N2 fixation by Trichodesmium (Mulholland et al., 2006) and the trophic transfer of recently fixed N from Trichodesmium to co-occurring plankton (Mulholland et al., 2004a,b), and also estimate rates of pelagic N2 fixation concurrent with the development and persistence of Karenia brevis populations. Because it has been projected that N2 fixation will increase in response to elevated pCO2 and climate forcing (Hutchins et al., 2007, 2009; Levitan et al., 2007; Barcelos e Ramos et al., 2007), determining the present relationship between diazotrophic N inputs and productivity of planktonic food webs that include harmful algae is crucial for projecting the likelihood of blooms in the future.

Environmental Factors Controlling N_2 Fixation in Mediterranean Rice Fields A. Quesada, F. Leganés, E. Fernández-Valiente Dept. Biología, Universidad Autónoma de Madrid, 28049 Madrid, Spain Received 24 January 1996; Accepted: 11 June 1996 ABSTRACT The objectives of this study were to analyze the environmental controls on N_2 fixation in Spanish rice fields. Nitrogenase activity, measured as the acetylene-reducing activity (ARA), was estimated in situ during different intervals of the cropping period. At the same time, physical and chemical variables and cyanobacterial occurrence were determined in water and soil. Nitrogen fixation was measurable at all sampling sites, being higher in July and lower in June after a short dry period. The ARA values ranged from 0.23 to 75.5 kg N Na^{-1} year^{-1}. Because blooms or other conspicuous cyanobacterial forms were not included in the measurements, maximum rates of nitrogen fixation may have been higher. Environmental variables that correlated with ARA varied on a seasonal basis. Water properties such as calcium, hardness, or conductivity, and soil properties such as conductivity and sodium correlated positively with N_2 fixation; however, nutrient parameters such as dissolved inorganic nitrogen or soluble reactive phosphorus were negatively correlated. Cyanobacterial abundance, in general, did not correlate with ARA. The overall conclusion is that nitrogen fixation may be an important N input in the N cycle of rice fields, and could lessen pollution problems by lowering the demand for chemical fertilizers. Introduction Rice fields are aquatic ecosystems subjected to a diversity of human modifications related to agricultural practices: flooding, drying, applying fertilizers, pesticides, and so forth. These practices may influence the microbial community composition and activities. The elemental cycles of this ecosystem may also be altered by changes in the nutrient loading and the physical and chemical properties of the habitat. N_2-fixing cyanobacteria constitute a major microbial component of the paddy field ecosystem and have been described as being responsible for spontaneous fertilization in rice fields [4]. The agronomical and ecological role of N_2 fixation in this agro-ecosystem has been broadly shown (e.g., [30]). Estimates of N fixed on a per crop basis range from less than 5 to more than 80 kg N ha^{-1} crop^{-1} [29]. The average value for oriental rice fields is around 30 kg N ha^{-1} crop^{-1} [30]. Much effort has been made to understand, and to promote, N_2 fixation in rice fields to maximize harvests without necessitating addition of N fertilizer. However, results have not always been successful [29] since the lack of extensive ecological studies (e.g., [10]) has not provided a fundamental knowledge of the microbial processes driving this ecosystem. Furthermore, most ecological work conducted on rice fields has examined the correlations between N_2-fixing microorganisms and environmental variables such as light, temperature, desiccation, etc. ([30] and references therein). Correlations between ARA and the physical and chemical properties of this agro-ecosystem are very scarce and have been conducted mainly with soil characteristics [38]. Water properties have seldom been investigated in rice fields (e.g. [37]). Rother et al. [34] studied N_2 fixation and some water features, namely, dissolved oxygen concentration, light (photosynthetic active radiation [PAR]), and temperature. Nitrogen fixation, usually measured as acetylene-reducing activity (ARA), has been measured in other aquatic ecosystems and is known to be an important input of nitrogen into the food web [14]. Nevertheless, the results have been contradictory; values obtained have ranged over three orders of magnitude. Some investigators propose that N_2 fixation may be controlled by single elements: primarily N inhibiting the activity [13] and P stimulating the fixation (e.g., [36]). It has also been suggested that the N/P ratio is related to ARA [12]. Marino et al. [20] suggested that the SO_4^{2-}/Mo ratio may control the abundance of nitrogen fixing cyanobacteria, although Paulsen et al. [22] have cast doubt on that hypothesis. Paerl et al. [21] have suggested physical conditions, i.e., turbulence, can be a key factor controlling nitrogenase activity in some N_2-fixing, but nonheterocystous, cyanobacterial communities (Trichodesmium). This work was conducted as part of a broader project whose aim was to evaluate the role of N_2 fixation as a natural fertilization system for the Valencian rice fields. Physical and chemical characteristics of the water and sediments from Valencian rice fields over a three-year period were described in detail in previous papers [27, 28], as well as the occurrence of cyanobacteria in this ecosystem [25]. The objectives of this study were (1) to evaluate nitrogen fixation over a large area of rice fields surroundings the La Albufera coastal lagoon, in order to determine the significance of this process, (2) to determine the physical and chemical features that control the nitrogenase activity in rice fields, and (3) to investigate the potential of nitrogen fixation as a method of biological fertilization. Materials and Methods The study area was located in the Iberian Peninsula, surrounding a coastal lagoon (La Albufera) near Valencia, Spain. Flood water comes from three primary sources: the Jucar River, urban and industrial wastewater, and water pumped from the coastal lagoon. However, in some sites, water was an indeterminate mixture of the three. Although the fertilization applied varied among farmers, rice fields were typically fertilized with 140 kg N ha^{-1} year^{-1}, as (NH_4)_2SO_4 at the beginning of the cropping season (May). A more detailed description of the sampling area and the rice crop cycle is given elsewhere [27]. The rice fields studied cover approximately 13,500 ha. Twenty-five sampling sites were distributed along several transects, covering the study area (Fig. 1). Sampling was conducted in 1989, during three different crop stages: May, after flooding; June, after a short dry period; and July, when plants are on average 80 cm tall. At each sampling site, water and sediment cores were taken to determine select physical and chemical characteristics of the water (May, June, July) and sediment (May). The ARA and heterocystous cyanobacterial abundance were determined for each sampling period, at every site, in triplicates. ![Map of the sampling area. Scale bar = 1.5 km.](page_1012_1042_1012_1012.png) Fig. 1. Map of the sampling area. Scale bar = 1.5 km. Water was collected in 1-liter polyethylene, wide-mouth jars. Soil cores were collected with a plexiglass cylinder, closing both ends with rubber stoppers to avoid disturbing the water-sediment interface. The water column was removed by gentle aspiration with a 100-ml syringe. The cores were then pushed with a Teflon pestle, and the first 0.5 cm was removed using a razor blade. Heterocystous cyanobacteria were enumerated by the dilution-plating technique. A more detailed description of the counting method may be found in Quesada and Fernández-Valiente [25]. Physico-chemical features of rice field water were analyzed in the field immediately after collection with the portable laboratory DREL 5 (Hach Company, USA). Most of the methods are adapted from Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater [2]. For details, see Quesada et al. [27]. Soil characteristics were measured on 10-cm cores (depth), after drying and grinding with a mortar and pestle. C and N contents were determined by an elemental analyzer (Perkin-Elmer 2400 CHN, USA). Ions (phosphate, Na^+, K^+) were extracted with an electro-ultrafiltration (EUF) system (Vogel 724, Germany). Analytical procedures are described, in depth, in Quesada et al. [28]. Nitrogenase activity was measured in situ using ARA assays, following the method described in Quesada et al. [26]. The method consists of using a bottomless, transparent, incubation chamber partially buried in the sediment, with an agitation system inside consisting of a rod and a clamp holder designed to support a motor supplied with a screw propeller. The agitation system allowed for measurement of ARA over 4 h with a minimum disturbance of the ecosystem. The assay was started by substituting acetylene for 10% of atmosphere inside the assay chamber. After the incubation, gas mixture aliquots were taken using a double needle connected to preevacuated Vacutainer tubes. Ethylene produced by nitrogenase reduction of acetylene was measured using gas chromatography. Spearman rank order correlations were performed to examine relationships between variables since the data usually were not normally distributed. Forward and/or backward stepwise multiple regressions were used to determine the cluster of variables that best explained the nitrogenase activity (transformed to log (nitrogenase)). Results Temporal and Spatial Distribution of Activity Incubation chambers for ARA were prepared with a rice plant cut to the water surface height. Incubations were performed during the day (between 9:00 and 19:00). Assay chambers were installed where no cyanobacterial presence was visually apparent, although separate experiments were conducted with cyanobacterial blooms. At each sampling site, one chamber without acetylene was placed to measure the background ethylene concentrations. At approximately 20% of the sites (primarily in June), the ethylene concentration was not considered to be a result of acetylene reduction since environmental ethylene was in the same range. ![Bar graph showing acetylene reducing activity at various sampling sites and times](page_1042_180_1012_670.png) Fig. 2. Acetylene reducing activity measured in situ during 1989. Units are in \( \mu \)mol ethylene \( m^{-2} h^{-1} \). The \( y \)-axis scale has been cut in order to better distinguish the lower values. Nitrogenase activity values higher than scale have been indicated. During each sampling period, dark assay chambers (covered with aluminium foil) were constructed in order to study the light dependence of ARA. The dark chambers were set up 3 h prior to acetylene addition. In every case, the ethylene increase in dark chambers was within the same range as that found in chambers without acetylene. Transparent incubators at the same site showed higher ethylene accumulation, suggesting a photodependence for nitrogenase activity. No consistent patterns in ARA, determined in situ, were evident throughout the sampling area, although, on average, sites from U to Z had higher values than the rest of sites (Fig. 2). The maximum mean activity (108.7 \( \mu \)mol ethylene \( m^{-2} h^{-1} \)) was obtained in July, and was tenfold higher than the values obtained in June (Table 1). In May, ARA values were high, but still lower than those observed in July. The standard deviation was always higher than the mean (Table 1), demonstrating the high variability in ARA found within the Valencian rice fields. The number of sites with low ARA values was similar during the three sampling periods (Table 1). Nevertheless, the frequency of sites with high ARA values was different between sampling periods. In May and July, 7 and 11 sites, respectively, showed high activities, \( >40 \) \( \mu \)mol ethylene \( m^{-2} h^{-1} \), while, in June, just one site reached that level. There were no sampling locations with consistently high or low ARA over the three sampling periods. All sites showed ARA values higher than the detection limit (estimated at 2 \( \mu \)mol ethylene \( m^{-2} h^{-1} \)) in at least one sampling period, and 95% of the sites had values above detection in at least two of the sampling periods. Results from experiments with cyanobacterial blooms are not presented, since, generally, they were not predictable events. ARA measured on blooms reached 2,500 μmol ethylene m⁻² h⁻¹, a value 40-fold higher than the mean values and twofold higher than the maximum value obtained when no bloom was visible. Assuming a ratio of acetylene reduced to N₂ fixed of 5:1 [33], then nitrogenase activity during 1 h at 12:00 is 8.3% of the total fixation throughout the day [33]. Also, assuming that nitrogen fixation occurs only during the rice cropping season (lasting for 137 days), ARA can be estimated as kg N ha⁻¹ year⁻¹. The estimate of the nitrogen fixed at each site ranged from 0.23 to 75.5 kg N ha⁻¹ year⁻¹, averaging 8.2 kg N ha⁻¹ year⁻¹ (standard deviation = 15.4, n = 25). When blooms were present, ARA reached 2 kg N ha⁻¹ day⁻¹. Water Properties and Nitrogenase Activity Table 2 shows a summary of physical and chemical properties of the rice field waters in 1989. Valencian rice field water may be generally described as hard, high conductivity, fresh water, with high levels of nutrients. For example, dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN) was between 1.75 mg l⁻¹ in July and 3.14 mg l⁻¹ in May, and soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) ranged up to 0.65 mg l⁻¹. A seasonal pattern was evident in variables such as O₂ concentration, percentage of light transmission, and pH, with higher values in May and relatively low ones in July. Spearman rank correlations between nitrogenase activity and the different physical and chemical variables measured in each sampling period are shown in Table 3. In May, there were more significant correlations between ARA and environmental variables than during the other sampling periods. Correlations in that month were positive with some of the water geochemical properties such as calcium, hardness, and conductivity, and the cyanobacterial abundance in soil. On the other hand, there were significant negative correlations with nitrate, dissolved inorganic nitrogen (DIN = NO₃⁻ + NH₄⁺) and the DIN/soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) ratio. Results from June showed that only N-nitrate and DIN were negatively correlated with ARA (the former with P < 0.05, and the second with P < 0.1). In July, results were different, and only two negative correlations with ARA were uncovered: P-phosphate (SRP) and cyanobacterial abundance in soil. Correlations of pooled data showed results similar to those found in May. Multiple regression analysis was performed to determine which properties could explain the most variability in ARA. In order to obtain normality, nitrogenase activities were log transformed. The results are summarized in Table 4. In May, conductivity, turbidity, and soil cyanobacterial abundance conformed to the multiple linear regression equation. In June, five of the variables (hardness, conductivity, pH, oxygen, and cyanobacterial abundance in water) accounted for approximately 50% of the ARA variability. Phosphate was the single variable that was included in the model for July, accounting for 53% of the ARA variability. When data were pooled, the regression model included conductivity, phosphate, and oxygen. To analyze which factors of the water chemistry predominantly influenced the conductivity, regression and correlation analyses were performed for water properties including calcium, chloride, hardness, sulfate, silicate, and up to 16 other ions, from the same sites and sampling periods as in 1989. Water conductivity was highly correlated with chloride, calcium, and sulfate (P < 0.005) only. Similar results were found by Alimagno and Yoshida [1] in Philippine rice fields. Other authors found increases in nitrogenase activity when transitioning from light to dark [34]. However, these studies did not utilize dark preincubations which have been described as necessary to promote the consumption of energy stores that are used to drive nitrogenase activity in the dark (e.g. [7]). The lack of common spatial and temporal patterns of N\(_2\) fixation is a recurring characteristic of biological activity in Spanish rice fields, and has been documented during other studies (e.g. [33]). The high variability (standard deviation always higher than the mean) may be caused by the effect of the different concentrations of the agriculture treatments at each site, or by the heterogeneous distribution of N\(_2\)-fixing microorganisms [32]. However, due to the large number of ARA determinations recorded, a representative pattern of nitrogen fixation in Valencian rice fields has evolved from this work. Seasonal variation of ARA is likely related to the agriculture practices of drying and flooding the fields, as indicated by the June sampling, when ARA values were minimal. The drying affects nitrogen fixation, although most of the heterocystous cyanobacteria are of the genus *Nostoc* [25], which is known for its ability to withstand desiccation [6].

Nitrogen fixation values found in Spanish rice fields are in the range of those published for rice fields of Asia and Africa, from less than 5 to 80 kg N ha\(^{-1}\) year\(^{-1}\) [30], but higher values have been described as well [31]. The average value (27 kg N ha\(^{-1}\) year\(^{-1}\)) is higher than that from our sampling area. In oceans, nitrogen fixation is usually estimated as less than 1 kg N ha\(^{-1}\) year\(^{-1}\) [14]. In estuaries, values range from the oceanic values to 8 kg N ha\(^{-1}\) year\(^{-1}\) [19]. Higher values are usually found in lakes, reaching levels of 90 kg N ha\(^{-1}\) year\(^{-1}\) in eutrophic lakes (e.g., [3]). N\(_2\) fixation values found in planktonic environments are believed to represent less than 10% of the N requirements by net primary producers ([14] and references therein). However, benthic N\(_2\) fixation seems to be important mainly in mats dominated by cyanobacteria, reaching values of 0.4 kg N ha\(^{-1}\) day\(^{-1}\) [17]. Because of the even distribution in mats, and the lack of continuity studies, previous estimations have to be regarded with caution. Moreover, it should be considered that the methodology and assumptions utilized in each study are different, and results may differ, as a consequence. Nutrient loading in the Valencian rice fields was an important factor influencing nitrogenase activity (Table 3). As many other authors have found (for review see [11]), high DIN concentrations inhibit, at least partially, nitrogenase activity. N concentration limits for ARA inhibition are vari- Fig. 4. Relationships between nitrogenase activity (as acetylene reducing activity) measured in situ in 1989 (May) and some soil properties. Total nitrogen (A) expressed as %, total P (B) and sodium (C) expressed as ppm, and conductivity (D) as \( \mu \)S cm\(^{-1}\). able, depending on the ecosystem, but DIN values around 0.1 mg l\(^{-1}\) are usually considered inhibitory (e.g., [13]). Our results showed a threshold effect, but this limit was ten times higher (about 1 mg l\(^{-1}\)) than that previously described. These results agree with laboratory experiments, conducted with cyanobacterial strains isolated from Valencian rice fields, in which nitrogenase activity was only partially inhibited (75%), with N-ammonium concentration as high as 2.8 mg l\(^{-1}\) [24]. The negative correlation found in the rice fields between SRP and ARA (Fig. 2B) contrasts with previous works in which weak positive correlations were found [14]. However, P enrichment in field experiments usually did not increase nitrogenase activity [11]. The N/P ratio has been described as a better predictor of nitrogenase activity in lakes than N or P [8]. However, we found a significant correlation between them only in May, with a threshold effect, below the Redfield ratio (7.6 in mass units), values of ARA were higher (data not shown). Strikingly, a variable more strongly correlated with ARA was conductivity of water and soil. This relationship, to our knowledge, had not been described previously with freshwater cyanobacteria. Our results indicated that water conductivity was correlated mainly with Cl\(^{-}\), Ca\(^{+}\), and sulfate. Thus, conductivity can be considered an indirect measurement of salinity. In marine cyanobacteria, the optimum salt concentration for ARA was found to be in the range for marine environments (e.g., [16]), and higher salinities inhibited cyanobacterial nitrogenase activity [23]. Quesada and Fernández-Valiente [25] found a positive correlation between cyanobacterial abundance and conductivity in Valencian rice fields. The observed ARA increase with moderate salinity could be explained by the increase of respiratory metabolism found in cyanobacteria under high salinity [15]. Increased metabolism would decrease the O\(_2\) concentration in the proximity of the nitrogenase site. As N\(_2\) fixation is an O\(_2\)-sensitive process [9], any mechanism reducing the O\(_2\) concentration may result in an increase in nitrogenase activity. Moreover, the direct relationship between ARA and conductivity could be based on the calcium component of conductivity since Ca\(^{2+}\) has been found to increase heterocyst frequency and nitrogenase activity in cyanobacteria [35]. Light intensity (PAR) does not seem to be a critical variable involved in controlling nitrogenase activity in Valencian rice fields, although a weak positive correlation was found with pooled data (Table 3). Rother et al. [34] did not find clear relationships between PAR and ARA in Bangladesh rice fields, although their data suggest an inhibitory effect on nitrogenase from 1,600 \( \mu \)mol photon m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\). Many papers have been published, from an agricultural point of view, correlating nitrogen fixation exclusively with soil characteristics (e.g., [38]). However, our data indicated that physical and chemical characteristics of water influenced nitrogen fixation more than the soil properties examined. Similar results were found by Quesada and Fernández-Valiente [25] studying cyanobacterial abundance. This may be due to the fact that most of the nitrogen-fixing microorganisms found in rice fields are photoautotrophic [30], thus, they inhabit the soil surface [39], and water features may directly influence their distribution. We did not find a consistent correlation pattern between ARA and heterocystous cyanobacteria abundance. There was a positive correlation in May but it was negative in July. Similar results were obtained when total cyanobacteria (from soil and water) in the incubation chamber were correlated with ARA (data not shown), since soil cyanobacteria contributed more than 99% to total cyanobacterial abundance. The relative contribution of epiphytic cyanobacteria to total abundance is unknown, and it could be the cause of the weak correlations. Furthermore, bacterial nitrogen fixation (phototrophic or even heterotrophic) may be of major importance in rice fields [18], although no information is available for Valencian rice fields. Moreover, the low accuracy of the counting method utilized (dilution plating), which does not typically represent the total population, could also be contributing to the weak correlations between ARA and cyanobacterial abundance. In fact, studies in progress indicate a more significant correlation between ARA and N\(_2\)-fixing cyanobacteria counted by direct fluorescence microscopy (Fernández-Valiente et al. in preparation). The relative importance of nitrogenase activity in the N cycle of the Valencian rice fields is difficult to estimate since most N requirements of primary producers are met by fertilization (up to 140 kg N ha\(^{-1}\) year\(^{-1}\)). At the ecosystem level, most of N losses are due, in addition to rice crop removal, to denitrification and to ammonium volatilization [5]. However, these have not been measured in Valencian rice fields. The apparently modest mean N\(_2\)-fixation recorded should be considered the minimum value for this region, since the incubation chamber was always placed where no apparent cyanobacterial biomass was present. If nitrogen fixation by cyanobacterial blooms was considered, N input would be much higher. Since their presence and duration was an unpredictable event in the rice fields, it has not been possible to globally estimate their contribution. Moreover, the assumption that nitrogen fixation takes place only during the cropping period (137 days) might not be accurate. In winter, there is at least one additional month of flooding with undescribed N\(_2\)-fixation, although limited data indicated modest N\(_2\)-fixation. Furthermore, in October, without flowing water, but with waterlogged sediments, numbers of heterocystous cyanobacteria were high [28], and fragmentary data indicated high N\(_2\)-fixing values (data not shown). Therefore, actual N\(_2\) fixation may be much higher than previously thought. Regardless, any natural nitrogen input to an agro-ecosystem such as the rice fields can be considered beneficial since it can decrease the fertilizer requirements. Summarizing, nitrogen fixation in Valencian rice fields is distributed over the whole crop period, with lower activity in June after the soil is dried and reflooded. Physical and chemical characteristics of water correlated better with ARA than selected soil properties. Significant correlations were found with N and P concentration (negatively), and conductivity (positively), although other variables such as calcium, DIN/SRP, and cyanobacterial abundance were weakly correlated with ARA. Mean values of nitrogen fixation were approximately 8 kg N ha\(^{-1}\) crop\(^{-1}\), although this is considered a conservative estimate. Actual values are likely to be much higher. OPEN Nitrogen Fixation by Trichodesmium and unicellular diazotrophs in the northern South China Sea and the Kuroshio in summer Chao Wu1, Fei-Xue Fu2, Jun Sun3,4, Satheeswaran Thangaraj3 & Laxman Pujari3 Distribution of diazotrophs and their nitrogen fixation activity were investigated in the northern South China Sea (nSCS) and the Kuroshio from July 16th to September 1st, 2009. N2 fixation activities in whole seawater and <10 μm fraction at the surface were measured by acetylene reduction assay. Higher activities were observed at the East China Sea (ECS) Kuroshio and the nSCS shelf. The nSCS basin showed a low N2 fixation activity. The <10 μm fractions (unicellular diazotrophs) contributed major portion to the whole-water activity in the survey time, indicating that nanoplanktonic cyanobacterias were the major diazotrophs in the survey area. Daily N2 fixation rates of Trichodesmium ranged from 0.11 to 9.83 pmolNtrichome−1 d−1 with an average of 4.03 pmolNtrichome−1 d−1. The Luzon Strait and the ECS Kuroshio had higher N2 fixation rates of Trichodesmium than the nSCS shelf and basin. Calculated activities of Trichodesmium at most stations were moderately low compared with that of the whole-water. The contribution of N2 fixation by the whole-water to primary production ranged from 1.7% to 18.5%. The estimated amount of new nitrogen introduced by Trichodesmium contributed up to 0.14% of the total primary production and 0.41% of the new production in the Luzon Strait. N2 fixation is an important process in adding “new” nitrogen to oligotrophic ocean ecosystems1. The current focus in assessing the global role of the upper ocean in sequestering atmospheric CO2 has elevated the importance of quantifying marine N2 fixation2. The filamentous non-heterocystous cyanobacteria Trichodesmium and diatom-diazotroph associations containing the cyanobiont Richelia intracellularis were traditionally considered to be the most important contributors to open-ocean N2 fixation. Trichodesmium mainly inhabits stratified, oligotrophic, tropical and subtropical oceans which are characterized by low nutrient concentrations, clear waters, and deep light penetration3–5. N2 fixation from Trichodesmium may supply up to half of the N required to sustain the rate of the annual particulate N (PN) export from the euphotic zone at Sta. ALOHA (22°45′N, 158°00′W) in the subtropical North Pacific Ocean6. However, the discovery of two unicellular diazotrophic cyanobacteria [UCYN group A (UCYN-A) and Crocosphaera watsonii (group B)], whose abundances and N2 fixation rates can be equal to or greater than those of Trichodesmium, demands the scientists to make a reassessment of the N inputs to the global ocean via N2 fixation7–9. The South China Sea (SCS) is the second largest marginal sea in the world. It is located in the tropical-subtropical western North Pacific and has a surface area of about 3.5 × 106 km2. Because of the effects of the monsoons and eddies, the northern SCS (nSCS) displays a complex hydrological and biological characters. The surface circulation of the nSCS changes seasonally in response to the prevalent monsoons. Overall seasonal circulation in the SCS is cyclonic in winter and anti-cyclonic in summer10. Upwellings and downwellings are forced by the interaction of monsoons and eddies11. The surface water of the nSCS and the Kuroshio is generally warm, stratified and oligotrophic which is supposedly an ideal habitat for N-fixers especially in summer4. The Kuroshio and nSCS are two neighboring and interacting waterbodies. The Kuroshio spans a wide range of latitudes from tropical 15°N to temperate 40°N. The upstream Kuroshio intrudes into the SCS through the Luzon Strait which is the deepest passage between the western Pacific and the SCS. It is suggested that the Kuroshio has a branch intruding into the nSCS in winter, but it sometimes intrudes into the nSCS in summer mostly in the form of “loop” and “extend”12,13. After passing southeastern Taiwan, the Kuroshio water flows northward and exchange their energy and matter with the East China Sea. The Kuroshio and the nSCS show different nutrient dynamics. Gong et al.14 observed that nutricline in the northern SCS is shallower than the Kuroshio14. Chen et al.15 also observed that in summer nitracline is shallower in the SCS than in the Kuroshio15. Most published studies of marine nitrogen fixation were focused on the North Pacific8,16–19 and North Atlantic20–23. Compared with previous studies in the East China Sea24, the SCS4,15,25 and the Kuroshio26 have been studied deficiently. The present study was conducted to investigate the horizontal and vertical variation of Trichodesmium abundance and it’s in situ nitrogen fixation rates in the nSCS and the Kuroshio. Size fractionation experiments were also conducted to compare the relative importance of the activity between different size classes of diazotrophs in the Kuroshio and nSCS. In addition, environmental factors were measured to determine the main ecological factors that control the nitrogen fixation. Results Hydrographic conditions. Most regions in nSCS were characterized by high temperature and high salinity (Fig. 1). In East China Sea, regions that heavily influenced by the Kuroshio also had high temperature and high salinity (Fig. 1). In nSCS during survey time, surface NO3− + NO2−, SRP, and silicate concentrations were lower than 0.15 μmol L−1, 0.1 μmol L−1, and 3 μmol L−1 respectively. Discussion In the summer, most regions of the nSCS have high SST except some regions which are influenced by the upstream. The stratified water of the nSCS results in the low supplement of the nutrient from deeper water. Originating from the southeast of Taiwan and east of the Luzon Strait, the Kuroshio is characterized by high temperature, high salinity, high transparency and low nutrients concentrations. As a result, most regions of the nSCS and the ECS Kuroshio were warm, stratified and oligotrophic which favored the growth of the diazotrophs. As an important diazotroph in the oligotrophic ocean and the Kuroshio water species indicator, Trichodesmium's distribution and nitrogen fixation rate in the nSCS and neighboring Kuroshio play an important role in the biological production, especially the new production of the SCS and the Kuroshio. Although conditions in both the SCS and the Kuroshio seem favorable for Trichodesmium growth, the Kuroshio had a higher abundance of Trichodesmium and nitrogen fixation rate than the nSCS. The standing crop and nitrogen fixation rate of Trichodesmium in the SCS basin is very low (Fig. 4 and Table 2). Shiozaki et al.26 suggested the high abundance of Trichodesmium in the ESC Kuroshio were ascribable to the supply of Trichodesmium spp. and other diazotrophs from the surrounding islands26. The Kuroshio is a western boundary current which originating from the southeast of Taiwan and east of the Luzon Strait, and enters the East China Sea (ECS) northeast of Taiwan. During our investigations, the surface abundance of Trichodesmium in Sta.E404 in the Luzon Strait was two orders of magnitude higher than stations in the nSCS and several times higher than stations in the ESC Kuroshio (Fig. 6). These results proved Trichodesmium spp. would likely to be transported to the mainstream of the Kuroshio from the Luzon Strait. Trichodesmium spp. were traditionally perceived to be the most abundant cyanobacteria in the marine, and it has been demonstrated to contribute the vast majority of N_2 fixation rates and primary production to the ocean3,42. However, increasing studies have shown that unicellular diazotrophs often appear to be of equal or greater abundance to the other known N_2 fixers due to the revolution use of polymerase chain reaction (PCR) techniques7,31. A DIC budget analysis at the SEATS in the SCS basin demonstrated that unicellular diazotrophs contributed enormously to the N_2 fixation, which were thus an indispensable part of the N cycle study in the SCS43. Chen et al.31 observed that unicellular diazotrophs contributed 65% and 50% of the total N_2 fixation in the SCS and the Kuroshio, respectively31. According to the results of size fractionation experiments in the present study, unicellular diazotrophs were important N_2 fixers in the surface of the nSCS and the Kuroshio. However, investigation on the distribution of the unicellular diazotrophs and their phylogenetic relationships with the unicellular diazotrophs from the tropical North Atlantic and Pacific oceans remain insufficient. Similar situation happens to Richelia intracellularis. Further studies of the other diazotrophs including their distribution and nitrogen fixation rate are needed in order to estimate the role of the N_2 fixation in the nutrient and carbon cycling in SCS and the Kuroshio. In the open ocean, many factors can influence the activity and diversity of diazotrophs. Water temperature is a major factor controlling the distribution of diazotrophs44. Trichodesmium is distributed where temperatures are between 20°C and 30°C and thrives when temperature is 25°C or warmer45,46. By comparison, unicellular diazotrophs often present in deeper and colder waters than Trichodesmium29. In the present study, however, the correlation between size-fractioned N_2 fixation and temperature was not significant in both the nSCS and the Kuroshio. This might be attributed to the unusually strong wind and highly turbulent surface during summer cruise31. Diazotrophs, especially Trichodesmium, usually thrives in relatively stable environment. Previous works had demonstrated the importance of wind as a driving force for promoting the growth of Trichodesmium and diatoms47,48. Generally it has been found that highest concentrations of Trichodesmium occur during prolonged calm wind (<10 knots ≈ 5.14 m/s) conditions whereas the highest diatom concentrations occur during windy (>15 knots ≈ 7.72 m/s) conditions. Calm waters with low turbulence benefit bundle formation and tend to enhance N_2 fixation4. During the survey time, influenced by the typhoon “Swan” and “Morakot”, a much lower abundance of Trichodesmium was detected at Sta. SEATS (1.08 × 10^3 trichomes m^{-2}) compared with the previous study4. Besides, diazotrophs growth rates are presumably limited by the availability of non-N nutrients, iron and phosphate are key factors limiting diazotrophs N_2 fixation and growth rates49. Iron is a important cofactor of nitrogenase, and it plays an crucial role in the synthesis and expression of nitrogenase in diazotrophs50. According to literatures, dissolved Fe (dFe) in surface waters ranged from 0.2–0.3 nmol L^{-1} in the SCS basin stations and 1.8–43.2 nmol L^{-1} in the northwest SCS coastal stations28,37. It was suggested that Fe availability may limit the rates of N_2 fixation in the SCS basin, while it was not happened in the nSCS coastal stations. As for the phosphate, it is a major component of cells which could also limit the growth of diazotrophs29,51. In the present study, the phosphate (P) concentration in most of the areas was very low or undetectable. However, both Trichodesmium and unicellular diazotrophs had form a number of mechanisms to overcome P limitation. A key characteristic of Trichodesmium is the presence of gas vesicles, which could provide buoyancy and help them migrate vertically in the water column to optimize light intensity or to obtain P and other nutrients from deep waters3. Unlike with Trichodesmium, unicellular diazotrophs could not migrate vertically in the water column, but they had been proved to own a robust capacity for scavenging phosphorus in oligotrophic systems due to the presence of high-affinity phosphate scavenging systems52. In addition, nitrogenase is instantaneously and irreversibly inactivated by oxygen, N_2 fixation is therefore a strictly anaerobic process53. However, many studies have demonstrated that both natural populations and laboratory cultures of Trichodesmium could fix N_2 exclusively in the daylight hours when photosynthetic activity takes place simultaneously54,55. Our result in Sta. PN04 and Sta. E404 also proved that Trichodesmium presented to be a daytime N_2 fixer. There are several hypotheses which aims to explain this phenomenon, but it is still an enigma how Trichodesmium can evolve O_2 while simultaneously fixing N_2. The most popular hypothesis is that Trichodesmium can use a combination of spatial and temporal separation strategy of N_2 fixation and photosynthesis within the photoperiod35,42,55. Staal et al.55 pointed that light stimulation of nitrogenase activity was most occurred at low O_2 concentration, while light stimulation became gradually less important at high O_2 concentration55. This result suggested the reduction of N_2 fixation in the latter stages of the light period was primarily attributed to the high net production of O_2 in the latter stages. Furthermore, nitrogenase activity can be recovered after a dark incubation when the cells were subsequently incubated in the light. Similarly, low O_2 concentration is in favor of the recovery of nitrogenase activity55. Our results were comparable with global ocean, and higher than other study in the same area which might be caused by the discrepancy between the two methods (Table 3). On the basis of a C: N = 6.6, N_2 fixation by the whole-water was calculated to contribute to 1.7% to 18.5% of the primary production in surface waters, suggesting that N_2 fixation plays a very important role in supporting surface phytoplankton N demand in some stations. Such values were exceeded the previous studies in the nSCS, and were comparable with N input by biological N_2 fixation in other oceans27,28,56. The variation of N_2 fixation rate by Trichodesmium was consistent with that of the standing crop of Trichodesmium. Conclusion In conclusion, the abundance of Trichodesmium were higher in the Luzon Strait and ECS Kuroshio than the nSCS shelf and basin, and so does the N2 fixation by Trichodesmium. It was suggested that the high abundance of Trichodesmium in the ECS Kuroshio were ascribable to the supply of Trichodesmium spp. and other diazotrophs from the surrounding islands. Nevertheless, it is still poorly understood and additional research is needed to resolve this question. According to the size-fractioned N2 fixation rates, unicellular diazotrophs also contributed significantly to N2 fixation in both the SCS and the Kuroshio. Further research should focus on the nitrogen and carbon biogeochemical cycles of unicellular diazotrophs in the SCS and the Kuroshio. Trichodesmium presented to be a daytime N2 fixer with the maximum N2 fixation rate in the 8:00 to 10:00 am and the rate decreased sharply as time goes by. Free trichomes were the absolute dominant population in the study area, and the radial colony and the longitudinal colony were also observed during the survey time which could be caused by the shortage of nutrient or trace element. The average number of trichomes per colony in present study was lower than values reported in other oceans, and the contribution of Trichodesmium to total Chla presented spatial difference which might be caused by the variation of their dominant phytoplankton. N2 fixation by the whole-water in some stations contributed a lot to primary production in surface waters, suggesting that N2 fixation plays a very important role in supporting surface phytoplankton N demand in these areas. Figure 8. Sampling stations of N₂ fixation rate. Note for software: Golden Software Surfer 11 (http://www.goldensoftware.com/). Materials and Methods Station locations and sampling. The study area was located between 15°N to 35°N and 105°E to 130°E (Fig. 8). A total of 13 sampling stations were studied during the summer of 2009. Surface water was collected using an HCl-rinsed bucket at all the stations. Vertical seawater was collected by using 30 L Go-Flo bottles attached to a rosette multi-sampler, on which the conductivity, temperature, and depth (CTD) probes were installed (Seabird SBE 9/11). Temperature and salinity were profiled vertically by the CTD profiler. Nutrients and Chl a measurements. Water samples for determination of nutrients were collected into 100 ml HCl-rinsed bottles and stored in 4 °C until analysis. Soluble reactive phosphate (SRP) concentrations were measured using standard molybdenum blue procedure57 or a home-made ship-board C18 enrichment-flow injection analysis system58,59. Nitrate and nitrite concentrations (NO₃⁻ + NO₂⁻) were measured by reducing NO₃⁻ to NO₂⁻ with a Cd column and then determining NO₂⁻ using the standard pink azo dye method and a flow injection analyzer60. Chl a samples were collected in 1 L bottles and then vacuum filtered (<10 mm Hg) through a 25 mm GF/F filter. Filters were kept in 10 mL vials and pigments were extracted with 90% acetone for 24 h inside a freezer at 4 °C. Chlorophyll concentrations of the extraction were then determined based on the fluorescence technique using a Trilogy (CHL NA, Model # 046) fluorometer on board. Trichodesmium enumeration and its contribution to Chl a. Water samples for determining the vertical distribution of Trichodesmium were collected from 25 m, 50 m, 75 m, 100 m and 150 m depths in each sampling station. Specimens for enumeration of Trichodesmium were prepared on board by filtering a 1–10 L water samples onto a 20 μm polycarbonate membrane filter (25 mm in diameter). Concentrations of the samples were fixed with 1% neutralized formaldehyde and preserved in the dark until analysis. Trichomes and colonies on the entire filter were counted under an inverted microscope. In order to determine the contribution of Trichodesmium to the total Chl a, 30–50 Trichodesmium colonies were picked up and washed in the filtered sea water. Then the chlorophyll concentrations of the colonies were measured using fluorescence method as described above. Primary production. Primary production (PP) was conducted according to Parsons et al.61 by ¹⁴C incubation method61. Seawater samples were collected from surface (Table 1) or five depths of the euphotic layer (Table 2), then prescreened through 200 μm mesh and filled into 250 mL acid-cleaned polycarbonate carboy (Nalgene; USA). Each sample was inoculated with 10 μCi NaH¹⁴CO₃ before incubation, and carboys which used for incubate subsurface samples were covered with the neutral density filter to simulate the in situ irradiance. Carboys were incubated in an on-deck incubator cooled by running water pumped up from a 5 m depth. After 4 h incubation, seawater samples were filtered through 25 mm diameter GF/F filters, and then the filters were placed in the aluminum foil bags and stored in the −20 °C freezer until analysis. In the laboratory, filters were fumed with HCl to remove residual inorganic carbon before they were moved into the scintillation vials, next the 10 mL scintillation cocktail (Ultima Gold; PerkinElmer; USA) were added. The activity of radioactive was counted using a Tri-Carb 2800TR liquid scintillation counter (Perkin-Elmer; USA). Size-fractioned N_2 fixation rates measurements. N_2 fixation activity was measured by acetylene reduction assay^3. Sampling stations were grouped into four sectors according to their bottom depths and locations (Fig. 8): the nSCS shelf (Sta. S209, E503 and D104), the nSCS basin (Sta. E607 and SEATS), the ECS Kuroshio (Sta. DH54 and PN04) and the Luzon Strait (Sta. E404 and E406). All experimental incubations were run in triplicate. 500 ml of surface seawater samples were introduced into a 600 mL HCl-rinsed polycarbonate bottles. After sealing with a butyl rubber stopper, 20 mL of acetylene was injected by replacing the same volume of headspace. Seawater samples that passed through a 10 μm mesh were also prepared for incubation of the surface samples in the same manner as whole seawater samples. Samples were incubated for 24 h in an on-deck incubator cooled by running water pumped up from a 5 m depth. At Sta. SEATS, subsurface samples were also obtained from 100%, 50%, 10%, 3% and 1% light depths relative to that of the surface to determine N_2 fixation at subsurface layers. The light intensity of the subsurface samples was adjusted to the in situ density using neutral density filters. N_2 fixation by Trichodesmium was also measured by acetylene reduction assay. A total of 6 sampling stations were occupied to determine the N_2 fixation rate of Trichodesmium (Fig. 8). Two sites were located in the ECS Kuroshio (Sta. PN04 and DH12), one site in the nSCS shelf (Sta. S209), one site in the Luzon Strait (Sta. E404) and two sites in the nSCS basin (Sta. SEATS and S504). Trichodesmium colonies were collected by a 76 μm mesh phytoplankton net towing gently in the surface water. Trichodesmium colonies were manually picked immediately by using a plastic bacteriological transfer loop and placed into a glass container with GF/F filtered seawater. Approximately 30–50 colonies were transferred to a 25 ml glass vial with 15 ml filtered seawater. The vials were sealed with butyl rubber stoppers. After injection of 2 ml acetylene, vials containing Trichodesmium colonies were incubated for 4–6 h in the daytime. To evaluate N_2 fixation of Trichodesmium, their activity at each station was calculated from their numerical abundance and their N_2 fixation activity per trichome. At the end of the incubation, the gas phase of the vials was sampled with a 100 μl gastight syringe (Agilent) and manually injected into a flame ionization gas chromatograph (GC6890N, Agilent). The temperatures of injector, detector and oven were set at 250 °C, 200 °C and 60 °C respectively. The carrier gas was helium at the highest purity available at a flow rate of 9 mlmin^{-1}. The supply of H_2 and air for the FID were 30 mlmin^{-1} and 300 mlmin^{-1}, respectively. The column was 20m-long wide-bore fused silica (0.53 mm inner diameter) packed with Porapak U (Agilent). The ethylene production during the incubation was calculated as Capone^62. The produced ethylene was converted to fixed nitrogen with a molar ratio of 4:1. After the assay, the incubated samples were fixed with 1% neutralized formaldehyde for the later enumeration of Trichodesmium.

The >10\( \mu \)m fractions N_2 fixation rates decreased with the light intensity except for the 10% light depth, while the <10\( \mu \)m fractions N_2 fixation rates increased with the light intensity in the middle three light depth. Light intensity is an important factor that determines the distribution of diazotrophs in the water column. *Trichodesmium* usually prefers the top sunlight of 75 m, but unicellular cyanobacteria tend to appear at deeper layers and down up to ~150 m\(^{29}\). The <10\( \mu \)m fractions N_2 fixation rate of 100% and 1% light depth were undetectable in our study. The rare occurrence of unicellular cyanobacteria at the SEATS station has been verified by molecular study\(^{30}\). The growth of unicellular cyanobacteria in this station could be limited by iron resources due to the competition from non-diazotrophs. The maximum whole-water N_2 fixation rate was observed in the 10% light depths in our study, and the result was different from the previous study that the maximum N_2 fixation was in the surface layer and decreasing with depth in the lower euphotic zone\(^{31}\). Notably, the main factor resulted in this situation was the N_2 fixation rate by >10\( \mu \)m fractions in the 10% light depths were larger than other depths extraordinarily. The same phenomenon was also observed in the nSCS\(^{15}\) and North Pacific\(^{32}\). A possible reason generated for this phenomenon probably due to the result of the downward flux of *Trichodesmium* spp\(^{33}\).

A time-series assay was also conducted at Sta. E404. N_2 fixation rates by Trichodesmium radial colonies were measured at 8:00–10:00, 10:00–14:00, 14:00–16:00 and 16:00–18:00. The maximum N_2 fixation rate occurred in the 8:00 to 10:00 am. The N_2 fixation rate by Trichodesmium decreased sharply from 8:00 am to 6:00 pm, and the rate dropped off rapidly to near zero prior to the onset of the dark period. The N_2 fixation rate during 4:00 to 6:00 pm was almost undetectable (Fig. 5). The results generated from field incubation were consistent with previous study that high N_2 fixation rates were measured for ~6 hours surrounding the middle of the photoperiod and N_2 fixation declined sharply in the latter light period^{35}.

Trichodesmium standing crop and their contribution to total Chl \( \alpha \). In most instances, the individual free trichomes were the absolute dominant population in global ocean^{4}. These free trichomes could form macroscopic colonies or aggregates which known as ‘puffs’ and ‘tufts’ in extreme oligotrophic conditions^{36}. In the present study, three living forms of Trichodesmium were observed during the survey time: the free trichome, the radial colony and the longitudinal colony. Likewise, the primary form of Trichodesmium in most stations were free living trichomes rather than colonies. This trait was in better agreement with previous study of Trichodesmium in the SCS and southern ECS^{4,37}.

The average number of trichomes per radial colony and longitudinal colony in all stations were 80 and 24, respectively. The average number of cells per trichome was 60. This data was typically higher than previous reports in the SCS that colonial forms of Trichodesmium were usually composed of less than 10 trichomes per colony^{37}. Our values were nevertheless lower than other oceans such as tropical North Atlantic Ocean (mean = 98 ± 11, range = 5–153 spp./colony), station ALOHA in subtropical eastern North Pacific Ocean (mean = 182, range = 10–375 spp./colony) and subtropical eastern North Atlantic gyre (mean = 112 ± 47 for puffs and 49 ± 16 for tufts, range = 57–156 for puffs and 31–63 for tufts spp./colony)^{38–40}. Trichodesmium integrated concentrations ranged from 2.18 to 726.17 × 10^3 trichomes m^{-2} and the average was 177.65 × 10^3 trichomes m^{-2}. The Luzon Strait and the ECS Kuroshio had higher Trichodesmium abundances than the nSCS shelf and basin. Vertical distribution of Trichodesmium showed that from the surface to the bottom the abundances of Trichodesmium decreased dramatically (Figs 5 and 6).

The values in the ECS Kuroshio and the Luzon Strait were significantly higher than that in the nSCS. Likewise, obvious spatial difference was also observed in another ocean.
