The relative contributions of unicellular and filamentous diazotrophs to N₂ fixation in the South China Sea and the upstream Kuroshio Yuh-ling Lee Chen a,b,*, Houng-Yung Chen b,c, Yen-Huei Lin a, Tze-Ching Yong a, Yukiko Taniuchi a,1, Sing-how Tuo a a Department of Marine Biotechnology and Resources, National Sun Yat-sen University, Kaohsiung 80424, Taiwan b Asia-Pacific Ocean Research Center, National Sun Yat-sen University, Kaohsiung 80424, Taiwan c Department of Oceanography, National Sun Yat-sen University, Kaohsiung 80424, Taiwan A R T I C L E I N F O Article history: Received 19 July 2013 Received in revised form 5 November 2013 Accepted 25 November 2013 Available online 19 December 2013 Keywords: N₂-fixation rate Size fraction Unicellular diazotroph Filamentous diazotroph South China Sea Kuroshio A B S T R A C T We studied the seasonal, diel, and vertical distribution of phytoplankton N₂ fixation to understand the relative contributions of unicellular and filamentous nitrogen fixers (diazotrophs) to N₂ fixation and nitrogen recycling in the northern South China Sea (SCS) and the neighboring upstream Kuroshio. N₂-fixation rates were measured by the ¹⁵N₂ tracer technique (addition by bubble) on unicellular (< 10 or 20 μm) and the filamentous diazotrophs (> 10 or 20 μm, mostly Trichodesmium and Richelia) fractionated by 10- or 20-μm mesh sizes. The mean depth-integrated total (unicellular+filamentous) N₂-fixation rates in the SCS (51.7 ± 6.2 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹) averaged 1/3 of that in the Kuroshio (142.7 ± 29.6 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹), with higher rates in the winter than in other seasons in the SCS and the opposite seasonal pattern in the Kuroshio. Unicellular diazotrophs contributed 65% of the total N₂ fixation in the SCS, which were negatively correlated with surface temperature and, as for total N₂ fixation, were higher in the winter when Trichodesmium spp. were scarce. In comparison, the unicellular diazotrophs contributed 50% of total N₂ fixation in the Kuroshio, and their contributions were not significantly correlated with surface temperature. In both the SCS and the Kuroshio, the unicellular N₂ fixation was more important during the night than during the day, and in the deep euphotic layer than in the surface layer, even in the daytime. Our results show that the unicellular diazotrophs were important N₂ fixers and contributed significantly to N₂ fixation in the tropical marginal seas, more so in the SCS than the Kuroshio. 1. Introduction Nitrogen (N) is often the most limiting nutrient element needed for phytoplankton growth in surface water of low-latitude open oceans (Hecky and Kilham, 1988). The primary sources of nitrogen are mixing of deep nitrate-rich water, atmospheric deposition, surface runoff, and N₂ fixation (Zehr and Kudela, 2011). In tropical–subtropical oceans, N₂ fixation often is a significant process of the N cycle that controls the productivity (Capone et al., 1997; Karl et al., 2002) and is an integral feature of the ecosystem function. Historically, N₂ fixation was believed to be primarily due to the filamentous nonheterocyst-forming cyanobacteria Trichodesmium spp. (hereafter Trichodesmium) with additional contributions by heterocyst-forming filamentous cyanobacterial symbionts of diatoms (Carpenter, 1983). Recently, however, rates of N₂ fixation by unicellular nitrogen fixers (diazotrophs) have been reported that equal or exceed those of filamentous diazotrophs Trichodesmium in some parts of the ocean (Montoya et al., 2004; Zehr et al., 2007). The South China Sea (SCS) and the neighboring upstream Kuroshio (Fig. 1) are two interacting water bodies in the western North Pacific. The SCS basin is as much as 5000 m deep and is one of the major marginal seas on Earth. Its oceanography is heavily influenced by monsoons; the winter- and spring-prevailing north-eastern monsoon corresponds to the formation of cyclonic gyres and the summer- and autumn-prevailing southwestern monsoon creates anticyclonic gyres (Liu et al., 2002). The same monsoons also strongly influence the upstream Kuroshio. The Luzon Strait is the deepest passage between the western Pacific and the SCS, through which a branch of the Kuroshio intrudes into the northern SCS. As the Kuroshio enters the SCS, the ensuing upwelling brings nutrient-laden subsurface water closer to the surface. Although the upstream Kuroshio and the SCS basin are typical of tropical or subtropical environments, a shallower nitracline in the SCS (Chen et al., 2003) indicates that more nitrate is available for phytoplankton there than in the Kuroshio. Fig. 1. Bottom topography and locations of the sampling stations in the South China Sea (Sts. S1–S7) and upstream Kuroshio (Sts. K1–K5). S7 is the South East Asia Time Series Station (SEATS). Inset shows the mean Kuroshio path (after Qiu, 2008) along the North Pacific west boundary. The seasonal dynamics of Trichodesmium abundance in the SCS and the upstream Kuroshio have been well studied. In the summer, although the oceanic conditions in the two regions are favorable for the growth of Trichodesmium, they are much more abundant in the Kuroshio than the SCS. The standing crop of Trichodesmium in the SCS basin (0.2–4.9 × 10^6 trichomes m^{-2}) is surprisingly low when compared to that (0.5–346.1 × 10^6) in the Kuroshio (Chen et al., 2008). Although Wu et al. (2003) attributed iron deficiency from a lack of organic ligands for the low Trichodesmium abundance, Chen et al. (2003) suggested that the reason was a shallow nitracline in the SCS. The abundances of Trichodesmium in the two regions have similar seasonal trends, being higher in summer than winter (Chen et al., 2008). This seasonal trend, however, is not consistent with that deduced from a biogeochemical study by Wong et al. (2002). Based on the calculation of the N anomaly (N^*), the authors suggested that N_2-fixation rates in the SCS should be higher in the northeastern monsoon season (winter) than in the southwestern monsoon season (summer). In addition to Trichodesmium, the filamentous cyanobacteria Richelia intracellularis (hereafter Richelia) and Calothrix rhizosoleniae (hereafter Calothrix) also contribute to N_2 fixation. Richelia and Calothrix contain heterocysts and are often symbiotic with diatoms. While Richelia lives inside the cells of several host diatoms, such as Rhizosolenia spp., Guinardia cylindrus, and Hemiaulus spp., Calothrix attaches epiphytically to host diatoms such as Chaetoceros compressus or Bacteriastrum spp. (Venrick, 1974; Villareal, 1992; Gómez et al., 2005). Although Trichodesmium is generally regarded to be the primary diazotroph, the relative contributions to N_2-fixation rates from other diazotrophs, especially the unicellular diazotrophs that have relative small sizes, could be significant. A study in the tropical North Atlantic Ocean revealed that unicellular diazotrophs and Trichodesmium contributed almost equally to the N_2-fixation rates (Falcón et al., 2004). As in most other oceans of the world, the distribution and N_2-fixation rates of unicellular diazotrophs in the SCS have not been systematically studied. Estimating their importance could answer questions relating to nitrogen cycling and oceanic production, such as the discrepancy between the N anomaly derived from the biogeochemical calculations and the Trichodesmium abundance. The existence of unicellular diazotrophs in the SCS has been confirmed by microscopic inspection of the unicells using the immunofluorescent method that detects nitrogenase (Chou et al., 2006) and also by molecular genetic analysis detecting the nifH genes (Moisander et al., 2008; Grosse et al., 2010; Bombar et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011); however, their rates of N_2 fixation and seasonal variations have not yet been measured.

It has been a common practice to size-fraction the diazotrophs into two fractions, < 10 μm (small fraction) and > 10 μm (large fraction), respectively, when the relative importance of unicellular and filamentous diazotrophs in contributing to N_2-fixation was studied. The large fraction is mainly composed of filamentous diazotrophs, including colonial, filamentous non-heterocystous such as Trichodesmium spp. and heterocystous cyanobacteria such as Richelia intracellularis. The small fraction is composed of a diverse community of unicellular diazotrophs, including N_2 fixing cyanobacteria (UCYN-A, -B and -C), heterotrophic bacteria and archaea (Kong et al., 2011). This study investigated (1) the seasonal dynamics of N_2 fixation rates in the SCS, especially the fractions derived from unicellular diazotrophs; (2) the relative contributions of unicellular diazotrophs versus filamentous diazotrophs to N_2 fixation in the SCS and the Kuroshio; and (3) the environmental factors that influence the dynamics of N_2-fixation rates in the two oceanic regions. The results are important in elucidating the nitrogen and carbon cycles and the functioning of the SCS and the Kuroshio ecosystems. 2. Materials and methods 2.1. Sampling and water chemistry This study was conducted during 8 cruises (Table 1) in the northern South China Sea (SCS) and the upstream Kuroshio (Fig. 1) between April 2008 and December 2010. Separated by latitude 121°E, 6 stations (S1–S6) in the northern SCS were located between 21°N and 21.5°N, and 5 Kuroshio stations (K1–K5) were between 21°N and 22°N. St. S7 at 18°N and 116°E is the South East Asia Time Series Station (SEATS). Some of the cruises were conducted during or shortly after tropical storms or when typhoons passed near the study area. Sampling in cruise CR910 (Table 1) was conducted 6 days after Typhoon Morakot made landfall on Taiwan and brought unprecedented rainfall to the southern island (2700 mm in 3 days, 1.7 times more than typical annually). Cruise CR1487 was conducted immediately after Typhoon Lionrock had passed near Sts. S1–S4, and as we sampled at Sts. S2 and S1, a second tropical storm, Typhoon Meranti, passed through Sts. S4–S5. We designated the cruises conducted in April–May, August, September, and December as spring, summer, autumn, and winter cruises, respectively (Table 1). In the analysis, we pooled the results of the spring, summer, and autumn as the warm season as the results of the ANOVA showed that in either the SCS or the Kuroshio, many variables including surfaced salinity, nitrate plus nitrite (N+N) concentration, soluble reactive phosphorus (SRP) concentration, chlorophyll a concentration (Chl a), depth of mixed layer (Dm), stratification index (SI) of water column, nitracline depth (Dni), or depth integrated abundances of Trichodesmium and Richelia were not significantly different among the three seasons. Seawater for nutrient analyses and biochemical measurements were collected (Table 1) from the six depths that corresponded to 100%, 46%, 38%, 13%, 6%, and 0.8% of surface irradiance by 20-l Go-Flo bottles on the CTD (Seabird SBE-9) rosette frame. Photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) was measured by a Biospherical sensor (OSP200L) on the CTD frame. Samples for Chl a (550 ml × 2 replicates), N+N, and SRP (100 ml × 2 replicates and 250 ml × 2 replicates) were sampled from the water bottles. Chl a was extracted from duplicate samples by acetone (Strickland and Parsons, 1972) and Chl a concentrations in the extracts were measured using a F3010 Hitachi fluorometer. N+N concentrations were measured by the chemiluminescent method (Garside, 1982) with a detection limit of 1–2 nM. SRP concentrations were measured at nanomolar concentrations by the modified-MAGIC (magnesium-induced co-precipitation) method (Thomson-Bullidis and Karl, 1998). SRP was corrected for arsenate interference and has a detection limit of 2–3 nM within the range of 10–50 nM. Depth of the euphotic zone (Deu, m) was defined as the depth at which light intensity was 0.8% of surface irradiance. Mixed layer depth (Dm, m) was defined as the depth of the layer of water having a density (\( \sigma_0 \)) gradient less than 0.1 kg m\(^{-4}\). The stratification index (SI, kg m\(^{-4}\)) was the averaged density difference between the surface and 100 m. Nitracline depth (Dni) was defined as the depth at which N+N concentration equaled 0.1 \( \mu \)M (Le Borgne et al., 2002) and Dni was used as an index of nitrate availability to phytoplankton in upper water column. It represents the stock concentration of surface nitrate as well as the upward diffusion potential of deep nitrate. 2.2. Measurement of \( N_2 \)-fixation rates Rates of \( N_2 \) fixation (\( ^{15}N_2 \) uptake) were measured using the stable isotope of N (\( ^{15}N_2 \)) following the tracer assay described by Montoya et al. (1996). The \( N_2 \)-fixation rate was partitioned into two fractions at the termination of the incubations by on-board filtration through 10-\( \mu \)m mesh during CR1487 and CR950 or 20-\( \mu \)m mesh for the earlier cruises. The filtrate passing through the meshes was regarded as the unicellular fraction, representing the contributions from unicellular diazotrophs. The difference between the whole seawater and the unicellular fraction was regarded as the filamentous fraction, representing the contribution from filamentous diazotrophs. Although most unicellular diazotrophs would be fractionated into the < 10 \( \mu \)m fraction, a mesh of 20 \( \mu \)m might be needed to fractionate all unicellular diazotrophs when unicellular cyanobacteria form large clusters in the samples (Falcón et al., 2004). Unfiltered seawater from the Go-Flo bottles was incubated in quadruplicate in gas-tight 4-l Nalgene polycarbonate bottles equipped with septum caps made of Teflon-lined butyl rubber. After filling, 8 ml of \( ^{15}N_2 \) (99 at%, Isotec, Sigma-Aldrich) were injected using a gas-tight syringe. Before the injection, a syringe tip was placed on the septum so that a same volume of water could be released out of the bottle with the injection of the \( ^{15}N_2 \) gas. Each bottle then was shaken for more than 5 times. Incubations were performed on deck under natural light in clear plastic incubators and temperature was controlled with circulation of flow-through surface seawater. During daytime, incubators were covered with one or more layers of neutral-density screen to attenuate the light to simulate the irradiances at the sampling depths. The 6% and 0.8% were covered additionally by a blue polyester film (ROSCO, USA) to simulate the light spectrum at the bottom of euphotic zone. At night, incubators were wrapped in black plastic sheets to block the incubations from the ship’s lights. Seawater samples typically were collected in the morning and evening. Samples were incubated for 7–10 h for daytime and nighttime incubations (Table 1). On cruises CR1487 and CR950, samples were incubated for 24 h. At the termination of all incubations, the samples in the two bottles designated to measure the overall \( N_2 \)-fixation rates were filtered under gentle vacuum through a pre-combusted (6 h at 450 °C) Whatman GF/F filter membrane. The samples in the other 2 bottles designated to measure the rates of the unicellular fraction were filtered first through the 10- or 20-\( \mu \)m meshes. The filtrate was then filtered through the pre-combusted GF/F membrane. The GF/F membranes were frozen at –20 °C and stored for further analysis. At the home laboratory, the membranes were acid-fumed with concentrated HCl for 2 h and dried in a vacuum desiccator. Each membrane was packed into a tin capsule and pelletized for isotopic analysis. Concentrations of particulate nitrogen and the isotopic ratios of \( ^{15}N \):\( ^{14}N \) were measured using a mass spectrometer (ANCA-MASS 20–20, Europa Scientific Ltd., Crewe, UK). Measurements of \( ^{15}N \) at% were reproducible at a precision of \( \pm 0.0003\% \). Daily \( N_2 \)-fixation rate was calculated assuming 12D:12N and using hourly rates obtained from daytime and nighttime incubations, respectively. No calculation was needed in the cases the incubations lasted for 24 h. Averaged daytime or nighttime \( N_2 \)-fixation rates were compared when both daytime and nighttime data were available. Depth-integrated \( N_2 \)-fixation rate was calculated by trapezoidal integration the measurements done from samples taken at different depths of the entire euphotic zone (100–0.8% surface irradiance). 2.3. Abundance of unicellular diazotrophs The abundances of unicellular diazotrophs were determined using the immunocytochemical method as described in Taniuchi et al. (2012). All specimens were collected during nighttime. Seawater samples from the Go-Flo bottles were pre-filtered on-board by 10- or 20-\( \mu \)m mesh to remove large plankton and then filtered on a 25-mm diameter, 1-\( \mu \)m polycarbonate membrane (Whatman, Kent, UK). The specimens then were fixed at 4 °C in 3% PFA (Paraformaldehyde, Nacalai tesque, Japan), preserved in 100% methanol and stored at –20 °C for later immunocytochemical examinations at the home laboratory. The immunocytochemical staining method was carried out following Taniuchi et al. (2008), using the antibody against nitrogenase of Trichodesmium sp. NIBB1067 (Ohki, 2008). Immunoreactions were visualized by incubating with DAB (3–3’-diaminobenzidine tetrahydrochloride hydrate, Sigma, USA) solution. Cells were enumerated at 1000 \( \times \) magnification under a Zeiss Axioskop microscope (Oberkochen, Germany). Depth-integrated the measurements on different depths in abundances of unicellular diazotrophs were calculated by trapezoidal integration of the entire euphotic zone. During cell enumerations, the cells were distinguished as coccoid or elliptical according to their cell shapes. The coccoid (C) cells were grouped as: < 1 μm (C < 1 μm), 1–3 μm (C1–3 μm), > 3 μm (C > 3 μm), and the elliptical cells were grouped as 1–3 μm (R1–3 μm) and > 3 μm (R > 3 μm). Enumeration on the 1-μm polycarbonate membrane of the unicellular diazotrophs might have missed the counting of some small sized organisms such as heterotrophic bacteria or UCYN-A, which were supposed to be contained in the measurements of N₂-fixation rates in which GF/F filters were used. 2.4. Abundance of Trichodesmium Specimens for enumeration of Trichodesmium were prepared on board by filtering 1.2- or 2.4-l seawater samples from the Go-Flo bottles through a 10-μm Nuclepore filter membrane (25-mm diameter). The filter membrane was laid on a microscope slide, and then a drop of immersion oil and a cover slip were added. Filters were frozen at −20 °C and stored in darkness for microscopic examination. All trichomes and colonies on each filter were counted (Carpenter et al., 1999) at magnification of 100–400 × using a Zeiss Axiovert 35 epifluorescence microscope with blue excitation (BP 450-490, FT 510, LP 520). Depth-integrated Trichodesmium abundance was calculated by trapezoidal integration from the surface to the depth of 0.8% surface irradiance and expressed as trichomes m⁻². Few Trichodesmium data (St. K4 of CR1310 and St. K5 of CR1316) from the Kuroshio were reported previously (Chen et al., 2011). 2.5. Abundance of Richelia and Calothrix The specimens that were prepared for the enumeration of Trichodesmium were used for enumeration of Richelia and Calothrix. The abundances of Richelia and Calothrix were obtained by counting the numbers of trichomes at a magnification of 100–400 × using a Zeiss Axiovert 35 epifluorescence microscope as the filaments of Richelia and Calothrix emit orange-yellow fluorescence under blue light excitation. In the analysis, Richelia and Calothrix were pooled as “Richelia” and thus the abundances of “Richelia” represent the abundances of Richelia plus Calothrix. Depth-integrated Richelia abundance was calculated by trapezoidal integration from the surface to the depth of 0.8% surface irradiance and expressed as trichomes m⁻². Few Richelia data (St. K4 of CR1310 and St. K5 of CR1316) from the Kuroshio were reported previously (Chen et al., 2011). 2.6. Checking the contamination by Trichodesmium in the small size fraction Although the unicellular fraction was designed to include only the unicellular diazotrophs, Trichodesmium however in the form of a single trichome appeared in this fraction, which would lead to an over-estimation of the unicellular contribution. We therefore examined all of the samples having a N₂-fixation rate higher for the unicellular fraction than for the filamentous fraction. An aliquot of 1.2-l of the preserved sample bulk seawater was filtered through a 10-μm or 20-μm mesh and then a 1-μm polycarbonate membrane (25 mm diameter, Whatman, Kent, UK). The numbers of Trichodesmium trichomes on the membrane were enumerated and designated as the abundances of Trichodesmium in the unicellular fraction. N₂-fixation rate of Trichodesmium in the unicellular fraction was calculated by multiplying the unit N₂-fixation rate of Trichodesmium trichomes in the filamentous fraction (assuming that the N₂-fixation rate in the filamentous fraction was only from Trichodesmium) with the abundance of Trichodesmium in the unicellular fraction. For the correction, this estimated value of the N₂-fixation rate for the Trichodesmium in the unicellular fraction, was subtracted from the rate of the unicellular fraction and added to the rate of the filamentous fraction. 2.7. Statistical analysis One-way ANOVA was conducted to compare the seasonal difference in the environmental variables and diazotroph abundances in the SCS and the Kuroshio. Regression analysis (Draper and Smith, 1981) were used to examine the relationships between N₂-fixation rates and abundances of diazotrophs, including Trichodesmium, Richelia, and unicellular diazotrophs, as well as the dynamics of environmental variables, including surface water temperature, salinity, Dm (mixed layer depth), SI (stratification index, the averaged density difference between the surface and 100 m), nitracline (depth where N+N concentration equals 0.1 μM), N+N, and SRP. Correlation coefficients among environmental variables were calculated. Mean N₂-fixation rates between the SCS and the Kuroshio were compared with t-tests for unicellular fraction and filamentous fraction, respectively. Depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates between the unicellular and the filamentous fractions were compared with paired t tests for the SCS and the Kuroshio, respectively. StatView programs (SAS Institute) were used to conduct the statistical procedures. Data are presented as mean ± standard error. 3. Results 3.1. Environmental variables The winter was a unique season in both the SCS and the Kuroshio. Many environmental variables, including surface water temperature, N+N, SRP, and Chl a, were different in the winter than the other 3 seasons (Table 2), which were collectively designated the “warm season”. All of the cruises conducted in the warm season were between mid-April and mid-September when the southwestern monsoon prevailed. In contrast, all of the winter cruises were conducted in December when the north-eastern monsoon prevailed. Yearly mean surface temperature was approximately 28.1 °C at both the SCS and the Kuroshio. Mean surface temperature was about 29 °C in the warm season and about 26 °C in the winter. Unlike surface temperature, annual mean surface salinity was lower in the SCS than the Kuroshio. Mean SI was higher in the SCS than the Kuroshio. Mean Dm was greater in the Kuroshio (89 m) than in the SCS (65 m). The mixed layer in the winter was deeper in the winter in the SCS and in the Kuroshio (80 m and 112 m, respectively) than in the warm season (59 m and 78 m, respectively). Similarly, mean surface water N+N and SRP concentrations were substantially higher in the winter than the warm season, especially the N+N concentrations. Mean N+N concentration was 204 nM in the winter and 20 nM in the warm season in the SCS, and 133 nM in the winter and 21 nM in the warm season in the Kuroshio. The depth of the nitracline also showed a great spatial difference in winter, 7 m in the SCS and 42 m in the Kuroshio, despite the fact that they differed little in the warm season. Mean surface water Chl a concentration was higher in the SCS (0.41 mg m⁻³) than in the Kuroshio (0.31 mg m⁻³) in the winter, but not different in the warm season. 3.2. The total depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates in the SCS were not significantly correlated with surface water temperature (Fig. 2A) (p=0.14). There was a tendency of higher rates in the winter than the warm season. Comparisons of the N₂-fixation rates between the two size fractions (Table 2) clearly revealed that N₂ fixation in the SCS was mostly by unicellular diazotrophs (t=1.86, p < 0.05, paired t test), which contributed 19.2–96.3% (mean 64.6 ± 6.8%) of the bulk seawater rate of the total depth-integrated N₂ fixation. This suggested that the contribution of unicellular diazotrophs was more important than filamentous diazotrophs, regardless of the difference of sample size among seasons. Occasionally, the N₂-fixation rates of filamentous diazotrophs were greater than those of unicellular diazotrophs, for example, Sts. S2 and S5 of CR910, which was conducted after a typhoon (Fig. 3A). The depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the filamentous fraction in the SCS ranged between 1.9 and 42.3 μmol N m−2 d−1 (mean 18.1 μmol N m−2 d−1) and were positively correlated with the abundances of Trichodesmium (p < 0.05, Fig. 4A) and Richelia (p < 0.01, Fig. 4B). The abundances of Trichodesmium and Richelia were weakly positively correlated (r=0.57, n=11, p=0.07, Fig. 4C). The depth-integrated abundances of Trichodesmium in the SCS ranged between 0.5 and 137 × 105 trichomes m−2 (mean 3.6 × 106 trichomes m−2), which were about 1/4 of those in the Kuroshio (Table 2). The depth-integrated abundances of Richelia in the SCS, ranging between 2 and 39 × 105 trichomes m−2 (mean 14.3 × 105 trichomes m−2), were not different from those in the Kuroshio (Table 2). The abundance of Richelia (trichomes m−2) in the SCS was about 40% of that of Trichodesmium. The lowest values of the depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the filamentous fraction (2.6–2.8 μmol N m−2 d−1) were measured at St. S2 during CR950 and S6 during CR1316, whose depth-integrated abundances of Trichodesmium (0.5–1.2 × 105 trichomes m−2) and Richelia (1.5–1.8 × 105 trichomes m−2) were also the lowest among the stations (Fig. 4C). The two stations (S2 and S5 during CR910) with the highest depth-integrated N₂ fixation rates of the filamentous fraction (32.5–42.3 μmol N m−2 d−1) also had the highest depth-integrated abundances of Trichodesmium (59–137 × 105 trichomes m−2) and Richelia (21–39 × 105 trichomes m−2) among the stations. In the SCS, the depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the unicellular fraction ranged between 10.0 and 73.1 μmol N m−2 d−1, with an overall mean of 33.6 μmol N m−2 d−1, which is about twice the rates of the filamentous fraction (Table 2). The rates of the unicellular fraction were negatively correlated (p=0.07) with the surface water temperature (Fig. 5). The highest rates were observed in the winter cruise CR950. High N₂-fixation rates were measured in the summer (CR1310) and autumn (CR1316) and low values were measured in the winter (CR886 and CR950), while the intermediate values were measured in the spring (CR1284). The two outliers that had low N₂-fixation rates in the warm season were probably caused by the influence of the typhoon (St. K1 of CR910) and the near-shore location of the station (St. K3 of CR1310) that had very low surface salinities. There was a clear seasonal difference in the Kuroshio in the relative importance of filamentous and unicellular diazotrophs contributions to N₂ fixation. In the warm season, the filamentous diazotrophs contributed more than did the unicellular diazotrophs (\( t = -3.54, p < 0.01 \), paired t test) (Fig. 3B). But the contributions of the two size fractions were not significantly different in the winter (\( t = 2.03, p = 0.07 \), paired t test). The proportion of the total N₂-fixation rate by the unicellular fraction was positively (\( p < 0.05 \)) correlated with surface water salinity (Fig. 3C). In the warm season, the N₂-fixation rate of the filamentous fraction was always greater than that of the unicellular fraction (Fig. 3B). Throughout the study, the N₂-fixation rate of the unicellular fraction was greater than that of the filamentous fraction in only a few instances in the winter (CR 886 and CR950). One exception, noted during CR910, was strongly influenced by the typhoon. The proportion of the assimilated \( ^{15}N_2 \) partitioned into the biomass of the unicellular fraction ranged between 22.4% and 89.2% with a mean of 49.7 \( \pm \) 5.9% of the bulk seawater rate (Table 2), indicating that the contributions of the unicellular and filamentous fractions were equal. In the Kuroshio, the depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the filamentous fraction were positively (\( p < 0.05 \)) correlated with surface water temperature (Fig. 6A) and to the abundance of Trichodesmium (Fig. 6B), but not to the abundance of Richelia (\( p > 0.05 \)). Among the filamentous diazotrophs, Trichodesmium was much more abundant than Richelia. The depth-integrated abundances of Trichodesmium ranged between 3 and \( 542 \times 10^5 \) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) (mean \( 144 \times 10^5 \) trichomes m\(^{-2}\)) and were about ten times those of Richelia, which ranged between 1 and \( 30 \times 10^5 \) trichomes m\(^{-2}\) (mean \( 14 \times 10^5 \) trichomes m\(^{-2}\); Table 2). The depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the filamentous fraction were low in winter, <50 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, coinciding with low abundances of *Trichodesmium* (3–37 × 10⁵ trichomes m⁻²). When the depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the filamentous fraction were high, as in the summer or autumn (100–190 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹), *Trichodesmium* was abundant (121–542 × 10⁵ trichomes m⁻²) (Fig. 6B). During the spring cruise CR1284, the depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the filamentous fraction ranged between the rates measured during the winter and the summer and autumn cruises, the depth-integrated abundance of *Trichodesmium* of the spring cruise ranged between 37 and 114 × 10⁵ trichomes m⁻², which was higher than that in the winter and lower than that in the summer and autumn. Exceptionally low depth-integrated rates of N₂-fixation of the filamentous fraction were observed at St. K1 during CR910 under the influence of a typhoon. Although the abundance of *Trichodesmium* was not low (Fig. 6B), the N₂-fixation rate of the filamentous fraction was very low, rendering this station an outlier from the common biomass–rate relationship (Fig. 6B). The salinities were unusually low in St. K1, <34.0 in the upper 18 m and lower from surface down to 100 m than the salinities frequently measured in the Kuroshio, such as St. K4 of CR1310 (Fig. 7A). Therefore, the T–S plot deviated from a typical Kuroshio T–S plot towards a typical SCS T–S plot (Fig. 7B), indicating a possible mixing of SCS water. Similar water mixing was reported by Chen et al. (2009), which they attributed to the entrainment of the relatively dilute SCS water in the Kuroshio as the typhoon passed. The N₂-fixation rates of the unicellular fraction rarely were greater than those of the filamentous fraction in the Kuroshio in the warm season. Another exception was St. K3 during the CR1310 cruise. Low depth-integrated rates of N₂ fixation of the filamentous fraction were measured at this near-shore station that had a surface salinity as low as 33.2. In the Kuroshio, the depth-integrated N₂-fixation rate of the unicellular fraction was positively (p < 0.05) correlated with the depth of the mixed layer (Fig. 8A) and to the depth-integrated abundance of the C < 3 μm group unicellular diazotrophs (Fig. 8B). As in the SCS, the unicellular diazotrophs in the Kuroshio, with the exception of the group C < 1 μm, were more abundant in the winter than in the warm season (Table 2). During CR950 in the winter, St. K2 had a deep mixing layer (178 m) and an abundant population of the C < 3 μm group unicellular diazotrophs. High depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the unicellular fraction, as much as 99 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, were measured at this station. Among all depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates of the unicellular fraction measured in this study, the highest rate (124–139 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹) was observed during CR1316 at Sts. K4–K5, where the mixed layer was 144–153 m. The lowest rate of 7.8 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹ was observed during CR1310 at St. K3, which had a shallow mixed layer of 31 m and also the highest stratification index. Comparison between the SCS and the Kuroshio During the warm season, the N_2-fixation rates in the Kuroshio were significantly higher than those in the SCS for both the unicellular diazotrophs (\( t = 2.87, p < 0.05 \), Fig. 9A) and the filamentous diazotrophs (\( t = 4.31, p < 0.01 \), Fig. 9B). The N_2-fixation rates in the Kuroshio averaged 66.1 \( \pm \) 14.5 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) for the unicellular diazotrophs, about 2.5 times those in the SCS (25.6 \( \pm \) 3.8 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)); for the filamentous diazotrophs, the Kuroshio was 6 times higher than in the SCS (114.4 \( \pm \) 21.7 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) and 19.7 \( \pm \) 5.0 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\), respectively) (Table 2). These differences between the SCS and the Kuroshio disappeared in winter. The wintertime N_2-fixation rates between the SCS and the Kuroshio varied little for either the unicellular (\( t = 0.62, p > 0.05 \)) or the filamentous diazotrophs (\( t = 0.50, p > 0.05 \)). The mean wintertime depth-integrated N_2-fixation rates of the filamentous diazotrophs in the SCS (13.9 \( \pm \) 5.7 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)) and the Kuroshio (17.9 \( \pm \) 9.3 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\)) were low (Fig. 9D) in comparison to the warm season. The mean wintertime depth-integrated N_2-fixation rates of the unicellular diazotrophs in the Kuroshio was 39.7 \( \pm \) 19.9 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) and 54.8 \( \pm \) 16.0 \( \mu \)mol N m\(^{-2}\) d\(^{-1}\) in the SCS (Fig. 9C). 3.5. Vertical profiles of N_2 fixation and abundances of filamentous and unicellular diazotrophs Mean N_2-fixation rates at various light depths were similar in the SCS (Fig. 10) and the Kuroshio (Fig. 11), regardless of size fractions or oceanic regions, in that most of the N_2 fixation occurred in the upper water column where light intensity was higher than 46% of surface PAR. The N_2-fixation rates decreased drastically below 46% PAR. The decrease of N_2-fixation rates from the surface (100% PAR) to the bottom (0.8% PAR) of the euphotic layer was less for the unicellular fraction than for the filamentous fraction (Figs. 10A vs. B and 11A vs. B), making the relative importance of the unicellular fraction increase with depth (Figs. 10D and 11D). In the SCS, the unicellular fraction contribution increased from 51% in the surface water to 73–82% at the light depths of 0.8–6% surface PAR (Fig. 10B). In the Kuroshio, the unicellular fraction contribution increased from 45% in the surface water to 93% at the bottom of the euphotic zone (Fig. 11B). The results suggest that unicellular diazotrophs’ share of contribution to N_2 fixation increased with increasing depth, even though the fixation rates decreased with depth (Figs. 10C and 11C). In the lower euphotic zone, the small sized unicellular diazotrophs were more important nitrogen fixers than the filamentous diazotrophs (Fig. 12). 3.6. Contamination by Trichodesmium in the small size fraction Although some Trichodesmium trichomes were in the unicellular fraction, Trichodesmium contamination did not change the dominance of unicellular diazotrophs in any sample we examined (Fig. 14). The contamination ranged between 1% and 8% in the SCS samples and 0% and 20% in the Kuroshio samples, except for two extreme values for St. S5 (34%) of CR910 and St. K5 (31%) of CR886. 4. Discussion 4.1. Comparisons of N₂-fixation rates The depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates in the Kuroshio, with a mean of 142.7 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹ and a range of 21.2–306.1 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, are comparable to the highest rates in the other oceanic regions of the world. Luo et al. (2012) summarized N₂-fixation rates in the global oceans and classified the western tropical Atlantic near the Caribbean Sea and the subtropical North Pacific near the Hawaiian Islands, with rates on the order of 100–1000 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, as the highest N₂ fixation regions. In contrast, the depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates in the northern SCS, with a mean of 51.7 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹ and a range of 18.1–85.6 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, is in the category with “most other regions” with ranges of 1–100 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, according to Luo et al. (2012). The mean surface N₂-fixation rates in the Kuroshio attributable to the unicellular fraction (1.19 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹) are slightly lower than those reported in the western equatorial Pacific (1.4 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹, Bonnet et al., 2009), but higher than most other tropical or subtropical oceanic regions, including the northern SCS of this study (0.56 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹), the ALOHA station (0.38 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹, Zehr et al., 2001; 0.16–0.55 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹, Dore et al., 2002), and the tropical North Atlantic (0.48 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹, Falcón et al., 2004). The most widely used method to measure oceanic N₂-fixation rates, as in the present study, uses ¹⁵N₂ gas as the tracer. Several recent studies indicated that this method underestimated true rates (Mohr et al., 2010; Großkopf et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012). This implies that most of the existing values of N₂-fixation rates are lower than the real values. Thus, our values of the N₂-fixation rates probably also are underestimates. Nevertheless the relative values and the conclusions drawn from size fraction comparisons, such as the relative importance of unicellular diazotrophs versus filamentous diazotrophs, remain valid. 4.2. Seasonal dynamics of N₂-fixation rates in the Kuroshio In both the SCS and the Kuroshio, seasonal changes in N₂-fixation rates were closely associated with the standing crops of their dominant diazotrophs. In the Kuroshio where Trichodesmium spp. were more abundant than in the SCS, both the N₂-fixation rates of bulk seawater and the filamentous fraction were correlated positively with surface temperature and were higher in the warm season than the winter. This seasonal trend agrees with previous Fig. 10. Vertical profiles in the euphotic zone of N_2-fixation rates of (A) unicellular fraction, (B) filamentous fraction, (C) total bulk sea water (unicellular+filamentous fractions), and (D) proportion of the unicellular fraction in the bulk seawater in the South China Sea. Data represents the mean and SE of N_2-fixation rates at each light penetration depth (LPD, in % of surface photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)). Waters were collected from each light penetration depth and incubated on board the ship at the simulated light intensities corresponding to its light penetration depth. CR indicates cruise numbers. observations in this study site (Chen et al., 2008) and elsewhere (Capone et al., 1997; Breitbarth et al., 2007) that filamentous *Trichodesmium* and *Richelia* usually are more abundant in warm waters than cold. 4.3. *Seasonal dynamics of N_2-fixation rates in the SCS* In contrast to the Kuroshio, unicellular diazotrophs were the major contributors to N_2 fixation in the northern SCS. Although the abundance of *Trichodesmium* in the SCS showed a similar seasonal trend as in the Kuroshio, their abundance on average was about 1/4 of those in the Kuroshio. The N_2-fixation rates of the unicellular fraction were higher in the winter than the warm season and were negatively correlated with surface temperature. The relationship of total N_2-fixation rates with water temperature was not significant, although the N_2-fixation rates of the filamentous fraction were significantly correlated with the abundances of *Trichodesmium* and *Richelia*. Because the surface temperatures of the two regions did not differ, water temperature alone cannot explain the regional differences in *Trichodesmium* abundance. A shortage of bioavailable iron (Wu et al., 2003) and competition for iron with flourishing non-diazotrophic organisms from an increased supply of advected nitrogen (Chen et al., 2008) have been hypothesized to limit the abundance of *Trichodesmium* in the SCS. Unicellular diazotrophs as the major contributors of N_2-fixation in the SCS, especially in the wintertime, explains the inconsistency raised by Wong et al. (2002), who found excess nitrogen, a nitrate anomaly (N*) as high as 2 \( \mu \)M, at the SEATS station in the winter, when the resident population and N_2 fixation of *Trichodesmium* is at the annual low. The authors postulated that the excess nitrogen might originate from sinking nitrogen-rich organic matter from surface diazotrophs and remineralization in the 150–500 m upper nutricline. Our study revealed that in the SCS, N_2 fixation could reach as deep as > 150 m, indicating that not all N* was from the surface N_2 fixation. In situ N_2 fixation by the unicellular diazotrophs residing at that depth could fix nitrogen and contribute to the N pool. The nitrogen fixed by the deep unicellular diazotrophs could be transported upwards to the euphotic layer through mixing from the northeastern monsoon or passage of typhoons and used by non-diazotrophic surface phytoplankton. The negative correlation of the unicellular fraction N_2-fixation rates and water temperature in the SCS (Fig. 5) pointed to a possibility that there was a certain abundance of group A (UCYN-A) unicellular diazotrophic cyanobacteria. Unicellular diazotrophs are composed of unicellular cyanobacteria, proteobacteria, and archaea (Zehr et al., 2001; Foster et al., 2007). Unicellular cyanobacteria, or UCYN, include 3 groups: UCYN-A, -B, and -C. In the present study, the method used to count unicellular diazotrophs could not distinguish clearly each of these groups. Quite a few studies however have investigated the relationships between Fig. 11. Vertical profiles in the euphotic zone of N_2-fixation rates of (A) unicellular fraction, (B) filamentous fraction, (C) total bulk sea water (unicellular + filamentous fractions), and (D) proportion of the unicellular fraction in the bulk seawater in the Kuroshio. Data represents the mean and SE of N_2-fixation rates at each light penetration depth (LPD, in % of surface photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)). Waters were collected from each light penetration depth and incubated on board the ship at the simulated light intensities corresponding to its light penetration depth. CR indicates cruise numbers. temperature and abundances of UCYNs, although none on proteobacteria or archaea. These studies have shown that UCYN-A are most abundant at 24 °C and UCYN-B at 29 °C (Moisander et al., 2010), while UCYN-C grow better in the laboratory at > 28 °C (Taniuchi et al., 2012). Based on these, we postulate that UCYN-A was likely the dominant unicellular diazotrophs in the winter in the northern SCS, in which the averaged temperature was 25.8 ± 0.6 °C, fairly closed to the temperature (24 °C) reported to support a flourishing UCYN-A population (Moisander et al., 2010). In addition, UCYN-A, as heterotrophs, depend on organic carbon (Zehr et al., 2008; Tripp et al., 2010) and symbiosis with other phytoplankton such as unicellular prymnesiophyte (Thompson et al., 2012). They would fare better trophically in the winter than the other seasons as the winter is the most productive season in the SCS (Chen et al., 2008). Conversely, in the Kuroshio temperature was not significantly related to N_2-fixation rates of the unicellular diazotrophs, which corresponded well with the relatively unproductive feature of the Kuroshio (Chen et al., 2008). Unlike the close quantitative relationships between the N_2-fixation rates of the filamentous fractions and the abundance of filamentous diazotrophs, there was no significant relationship between the N_2-fixation rates of the unicellular fractions and the abundance of unicellular diazotrophs. Although the real reason is yet to be unraveled, the high diversity of the unicellular diazotrophs and their mostly unknown respective biomass-specific N_2-fixation rates pose a great challenge in linking these factors. 4.4. Vertical profile of N_2-fixation rates The depth profiles of N_2-fixation rates in the Kuroshio and the northern SCS were similar to those in the ALOHA station (Grabowski et al., 2008; Church et al., 2009), showing a maximum in the surface layer and decreasing with depth in the lower euphotic zone. The high solar photon fluxes in the surface layer provide the high energy required for N_2 fixation (Karl et al., 2002). On the other hand, the increase in fixed N concentrations in the lower euphotic layer such as nitrate explain selection against N acquisition via N_2 fixation (Grabowski et al., 2008). Most Trichodesmium spp. are distributed in the surface water around 15–25 m depth because their cells contain gas vesicles that give positive buoyancy (Walsby, 1992). The result that the proportion of the unicellular fraction in the N_2-fixation rates increased with depth suggests that these depth-associated changes in temperature, light, or nutrient conditions might favor the growth of the unicellular diazotrophs. Similar to Trichodesmium, the depth of abundance maximum of Crocosphaera, a typical UCYN-B, is about 20 m, but that of UCYN-A is in significantly greater depth (Moisander et al., 2010). As photoheterotrophs, UCYN-A are also abundant in nitrate-rich estuarine waters (Short and Zehr, 2007), whose nutrient availabilities comparable to the lower euphotic zone. Because UCYN-B have been reported to distribute sparsely in the SCS (Zhang et al., 2011), the unicellular diazotrophs we observed in the lower euphotic zone of the SCS Fig. 12. Abundances of filamentous and unicellular diazotrophs at various light penetration depths (LPD, in % of surface photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)) in (A) and (B) the South China Sea (SCS) and (C) and (D) the Kuroshio. C indicates coccoid cells and R elliptical cells. Fig. 13. Daytime and nighttime- (A), (C) bulk seawater (unicellular fraction+filamentous fraction) N_2-fixation rates and (B), (D) proportions of the N_2-fixation rates by unicellular fraction (mean ± SE) at various light penetration depths (LPD, in % of surface photosynthetically active radiation (PAR)) in (A) and (B) the South China Sea (SCS) and (C) and (D) the Kuroshio. probably were UCYN-A, not UCYN-B, although the possibility of heterotrophic proteobacteria could not be ruled out. We know very little about the vertical distributions of proteobacteria in the ocean. Although both \( \alpha \)- and \( \gamma \)-proteobacteria could reside below the nutricline, \( \gamma \)-proteobacteria are confined mostly to the upper water. \( \alpha \)-Proteobacteria are distributed in the deeper water. In the SCS, \( \gamma \)-proteobacteria *nifH* was frequently detected in the upper 200 m, relatively less frequently below 450 m (*Zhang et al.*, 2011). In the water column off the Vietnamese coast, \( \gamma \)-proteobacteria also are distributed mostly in the euphotic layer, Fig. 14. Plots of depth-integrated (trapezoidal integration from various light penetration depths corresponding to 100–0.8% of surface PAR) N₂-fixation rates of the filamentous and unicellular fraction before (solid symbols) and after (open symbols) the correction for Trichodesmium contamination in the unicellular fraction of the samples from (A) the South China Sea (SCS) and (B) the Kuroshio. The 1:1 line indicates equal contribution to N₂-fixation rates by the unicellular fraction and filamentous fractions. while α-proteobacteria are distributed from the euphotic layer to mesopelagic depths (Moisander et al., 2008). In the Arabian Sea, γ-proteobacteria are distributed in the surface water and below the nutricline (Bird et al., 2005). A phylotype of α-proteobacteria also was identified in the deep hypoxic basins of the Southern California Bight at 350 m (Hamersley et al., 2011). Given these results, future studies on the rates and biology of N₂-fixation in the SCS and the Kuroshio should include water depths greater than 200 m. 4.5. Problems related to size fractionation Choosing a proper membrane or mesh and the pore size for filtration to ensure the satisfactory partition of filamentous and unicellular diazotrophs was difficult. In the preliminary experiments examining the seawater from the SCS, we used 47-mm diameter PC membranes with a 10-μm pore size. Many unicellular diazotrophs that were supposed to have passed the PC membrane were detected by the immunochemical method on the membranes, including about 27% of < 2 μm and 10% of > 2 μm rod-shaped diazotrophs, and 3% of < 2 μm and 7% of > 2 μm spherical diazotrophs. This indicates that these unicellular diazotrophs were recovered erroneously in the filamentous fraction and consequently would cause an underestimation of the contributions of the unicellular diazotrophs. Similarly, when Bonnet et al. (2009) used a 10-μm filter membrane for size fractionation, about 10% of picocyanodiazotrophs and nanocyanodiazotrophs were recovered in the > 10 μm fraction, overestimating N₂-fixation rate for the large size fraction. Although the large fraction were mainly composed of filamentous diazotrophs, some unicellular diazotrophs that formed colonies or associated with organisms > 10 or > 20 μm were recovered in the large size fraction. These include colonial forms of Crocosphaera watsonii (Biegala and Raimbault, 2008; Bonnet et al., 2009), some UCYN-A that form symbiosis with large phytoplankters (Thompson et al., 2012) and some particle-associated bacteria and archeae. In the present study, we used mesh instead of membrane for size fractionation. In doing this, we were able to obtain a more complete contribution for the unicellular diazotrophs. The risk that filamentous diazotrophs were recovered erroneously in the unicellular fraction, however, seemed unavoidable. When we checked the Trichodesmium contamination in the small size fraction, the results suggested that the contamination was limited. On the other hand, in the attempt to exclude the Trichodesmium contamination, we might have underestimated the contribution of the unicellular diazotrophs. Because the contribution of Richelia was not included in the correction, the N₂-fixation rates of Trichodesmium were overestimated when we divided the rate of the filamentous fraction solely by the abundance of Trichodesmium, exclusive of Richelia. Nevertheless, for every sample we examined, the correction for Trichodesmium contamination did not alter the conclusion. Another possible cause of erroneous estimation of the size fraction contribution might come from the release of labeled dissolved N by Trichodesmium (Mulholland and Capone, 2001; Mulholland et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2011) or unicellular diazotrophs (Benavides et al., 2011, 2013), which was not examined in the present study. We conducted the size fractionation after the incubation. This protocol has been widely used in studies relating to size fractionation for measurement of N₂-fixation rates, such as Dore et al. (2002), Grabowski et al. (2008); Bonnet et al. (2009, 2011); Church et al. (2009); Grosse et al. (2010); Hamersley et al. (2011); Watkins-Brandt et al. (2011). Using this protocol, the tracer \(^{15}\)N₂ fixed by diazotrophs during the incubation could be released to the media and re-absorbed by other large (such as diatoms, Chen et al., 2011) or small non-diazotrophic or diazotrophic phytoplankton. This could interfere the measurement of N₂-fixation rates from each size fraction. The interference could be lessened if size fractionation is conducted before the incubation instead of after (Kitajima et al., 2009; Benavides et al., 2011). However, the before-incubation size fractionation procedure might affect adversely some diazotrophs, such as Trichodesmium, and lead to a lower N₂-fixation rate. Future studies that compare the N₂-fixation rates with size fractionation procedures conducting before and after the incubation would help us to assess the extent of these errors in the study sites. 5. Conclusions In conclusion, unlike the Kuroshio where Trichodesmium was an important N₂-fixer, the major N₂-fixers in the SCS were unicellular diazotrophs. Also unlike the Kuroshio where N₂-fixation rates increased with increased temperature, N₂-fixation rates in the SCS were higher in the winter than the warm season. The unicellular diazotrophs dominating the nitrogen fixing population in the SCS were probably responsible for the high N₂-fixation rates, especially in the winter. As the driving force of N₂ fixation in the SCS, the unicellular diazotrophs clearly should be the focal point of studies of nitrogen and carbon biogeochemical cycles. Acknowledgments We thank L.F. The seasonal dynamics of Trichodesmium abundance in the SCS and the upstream Kuroshio have been well studied. In the summer, although the oceanic conditions in the two regions are favorable for the growth of Trichodesmium, they are much more abundant in the Kuroshio than the SCS. The standing crop of Trichodesmium in the SCS basin (0.2–4.9 × 10^6 trichomes m^{-2}) is surprisingly low when compared to that (0.5–346.1 × 10^6) in the Kuroshio (Chen et al., 2008). Although Wu et al. (2003) attributed iron deficiency from a lack of organic ligands for the low Trichodesmium abundance, Chen et al. (2003) suggested that the reason was a shallow nitracline in the SCS. The abundances of Trichodesmium in the two regions have similar seasonal trends, being higher in summer than winter (Chen et al., 2008). This seasonal trend, however, is not consistent with that deduced from a biogeochemical study by Wong et al. (2002). Based on the calculation of the N anomaly (N^*), the authors suggested that N_2-fixation rates in the SCS should be higher in the northeastern monsoon season (winter) than in the southwestern monsoon season (summer). In addition to Trichodesmium, the filamentous cyanobacteria Richelia intracellularis (hereafter Richelia) and Calothrix rhizosoleniae (hereafter Calothrix) also contribute to N_2 fixation. Richelia and Calothrix contain heterocysts and are often symbiotic with diatoms. While Richelia lives inside the cells of several host diatoms, such as Rhizosolenia spp., Guinardia cylindrus, and Hemiaulus spp., Calothrix attaches epiphytically to host diatoms such as Chaetoceros compressus or Bacteriastrum spp. (Venrick, 1974; Villareal, 1992; Gómez et al., 2005). Although Trichodesmium is generally regarded to be the primary diazotroph, the relative contributions to N_2-fixation rates from other diazotrophs, especially the unicellular diazotrophs that have relative small sizes, could be significant. A study in the tropical North Atlantic Ocean revealed that unicellular diazotrophs and Trichodesmium contributed almost equally to the N_2-fixation rates (Falcón et al., 2004). As in most other oceans of the world, the distribution and N_2-fixation rates of unicellular diazotrophs in the SCS have not been systematically studied. Estimating their importance could answer questions relating to nitrogen cycling and oceanic production, such as the discrepancy between the N anomaly derived from the biogeochemical calculations and the Trichodesmium abundance. The existence of unicellular diazotrophs in the SCS has been confirmed by microscopic inspection of the unicells using the immunofluorescent method that detects nitrogenase (Chou et al., 2006) and also by molecular genetic analysis detecting the nifH genes (Moisander et al., 2008; Grosse et al., 2010; Bombar et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2011); however, their rates of N_2 fixation and seasonal variations have not yet been measured.

It has been a common practice to size-fraction the diazotrophs into two fractions, < 10 μm (small fraction) and > 10 μm (large fraction), respectively, when the relative importance of unicellular and filamentous diazotrophs in contributing to N_2-fixation was studied. The large fraction is mainly composed of filamentous diazotrophs, including colonial, filamentous non-heterocystous such as Trichodesmium spp. and heterocystous cyanobacteria such as Richelia intracellularis. The small fraction is composed of a diverse community of unicellular diazotrophs, including N_2 fixing cyanobacteria (UCYN-A, -B and -C), heterotrophic bacteria and archaea (Kong et al., 2011). This study investigated (1) the seasonal dynamics of N_2 fixation rates in the SCS, especially the fractions derived from unicellular diazotrophs; (2) the relative contributions of unicellular diazotrophs versus filamentous diazotrophs to N_2 fixation in the SCS and the Kuroshio; and (3) the environmental factors that influence the dynamics of N_2-fixation rates in the two oceanic regions. N₂-fixation rates in the lower euphotic zone, regardless of daytime or nighttime, were mostly contributed by the unicellular diazotrophs.

3.7. Contamination by Trichodesmium in the small size fraction

Although some Trichodesmium trichomes were in the unicellular fraction, Trichodesmium contamination did not change the dominance of unicellular diazotrophs in any sample we examined (Fig. 14). The contamination ranged between 1% and 8% in the SCS samples and 0% and 20% in the Kuroshio samples, except for two extreme values for St. S5 (34%) of CR910 and St. K5 (31%) of CR886.

4. Discussion

4.1. Comparisons of N₂-fixation rates

The depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates in the Kuroshio, with a mean of 142.7 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹ and a range of 21.2–306.1 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, are comparable to the highest rates in the other oceanic regions of the world. Luo et al. (2012) summarized N₂-fixation rates in the global oceans and classified the western tropical Atlantic near the Caribbean Sea and the subtropical North Pacific near the Hawaiian Islands, with rates on the order of 100–1000 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, as the highest N₂ fixation regions. In contrast, the depth-integrated N₂-fixation rates in the northern SCS, with a mean of 51.7 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹ and a range of 18.1–85.6 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, is in the category with “most other regions” with ranges of 1–100 μmol N m⁻² d⁻¹, according to Luo et al. (2012).

The mean surface N₂-fixation rates in the Kuroshio attributable to the unicellular fraction (1.19 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹) are slightly lower than those reported in the western equatorial Pacific (1.4 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹, Bonnet et al., 2009), but higher than most other tropical or subtropical oceanic regions, including the northern SCS of this study (0.56 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹), the ALOHA station (0.38 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹, Zehr et al., 2001; 0.16–0.55 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹, Dore et al., 2002), and the tropical North Atlantic (0.48 nmol N l⁻¹ d⁻¹, Falcón et al., 2004).

The most widely used method to measure oceanic N₂-fixation rates, as in the present study, uses ¹⁵N₂ gas as the tracer. Several recent studies indicated that this method underestimated true rates (Mohr et al., 2010; Großkopf et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012). This implies that most of the existing values of N₂-fixation rates are lower than the real values. Thus, our values of the N₂-fixation rates probably also are underestimates. Nevertheless the relative values and the conclusions drawn from size fraction comparisons, such as the relative importance of unicellular diazotrophs versus filamentous diazotrophs, remain valid.

4.2. Seasonal dynamics of N₂-fixation rates in the Kuroshio

In both the SCS and the Kuroshio, seasonal changes in N₂-fixation rates were closely associated with the standing crops of their dominant diazotrophs. In the Kuroshio where Trichodesmium spp. were more abundant than in the SCS, both the N₂-fixation rates of bulk seawater and the filamentous fraction were correlated positively with surface temperature and were higher in the warm season than the winter. Stimulation of nitrogen fixation in refractory organic sediments by Caulerpa taxifolia (Chlorophyta) John R. M. Chisholm¹ and Pascale Moulin Observatoire Océanologique Européen, Centre Scientifique de Monaco, Avenue Saint Martin, MC 98000, Monaco Abstract Estimates of N₂ fixation by substrata associated with the rhizophytic alga Caulerpa taxifolia were obtained using the acetylene reduction method. On average, growth of C. taxifolia enhanced rates of acetylene reduction in underlying dead sea grass sediments by a factor of 28, although the degree of enhancement was variable. The average rate of ethylene production was 3.96 nmol cm⁻³ h⁻¹ (range = 2.5–6.2 nmol cm⁻³ h⁻¹). There was no apparent stimulation of N₂ fixation in substrata collected close to a wastewater outlet. C. taxifolia appears to enhance N₂ fixation by releasing photosynthetic product into the rhizosphere, mimicking the behavior of saltwater vascular plants. The excreted organic C activates the fermenting bacterial community, which in turn makes substrates available to the sulfate reducers. The associated microbial reactions create strong reducing conditions that favor N₂ fixation, of which many sulfate reducers are capable. Nitrogen fixation can serve to reduce the N deficit that inhibits bacterial decomposition of refractory sea grass waste, thereby enhancing organic matter turnover and nutrient supply to the alga’s rhizoids. This process likely assists C. taxifolia to proliferate upon refractory organic sediments in low-nutrient seawater. The green alga Caulerpa produces a pseudo-root system that functions to anchor the plant, as well as to take up nutrients (Williams 1984; Chisholm et al. 1996). Nutrient uptake from the substratum potentially enables the alga to proliferate in oligotrophic seawater on eutrophicated substrata (Chisholm et al. 1996). Biogeochemical studies in the northwest Mediterranean have indicated a link between the proliferation of Caulerpa taxifolia Vahl. C. (Agardh) and the availability of nutrients discharged in urban wastewater or resulting from the decay of sea grass vegetation (Chisholm et al. 1997). Association with wastewater pollution is not surprising because algal production has often been shown to increase with nutrient discharge. Association with decomposition of sea grass vegetation is less straightforward because sea grass tissues generally have low N content relative to C, which limits bacterial nutrient turnover (Goldman et al. 1987; Paerl 1990). Field and laboratory observations demonstrate that sediments containing dead sea grass matter frequently turn black in color after penetration by the rhizoids of C. taxifolia (Fig. 1). The black coloration is due to bacterial reduction of sulfate to sulfide, indicating strong reducing conditions that favor N₂ fixation. Nitrogen fixation could alleviate barriers to organic decomposition (Paerl 1990; Tibbles et al. 1994), thus enhancing nutrient supply to the alga’s rhizoids. C. taxifolia appears to activate the fermenting bacterial community into delivering secondary substrates to the sulfate reducers by releasing photosynthetic product from its rhizoids, as do salt marsh and sea grasses from their root systems (e.g., Pollard and Moriarty 1991; Welsh et al. 1997; Blaabjerg et al. 1998). Materials and methods We postulated that penetration of dead sea grass sediments by the rhizoids of C. taxifolia could enhance rates of N₂ fixation relative to uncolonized sea grass sediments and sediments fertilized by an external source of inorganic nitrogen. To test these postulates, we obtained sediments with and without C. taxifolia cover by SCUBA diving, on 1 October 2001 from (1) a dead bed of the sea grass Posidonia oceanica L. Delile near Cap Martin in southeast France and (2) close to the pretreatment and main sewer outlets for the Principality of Monaco (Fig. 2). Surface water samples collected at site 2 between July 2000 and July 2001 contained, on average, 4.2 μmol NO₃⁻ L⁻¹, 0.18 μmol NO₂⁻ L⁻¹, and 0.44 μmol NH₄⁺ L⁻¹ and maximum concentrations of 10.7 μmol NO₃⁻ L⁻¹, 0.40 μmol NO₂⁻ L⁻¹, and 1.44 μmol NH₄⁺ L⁻¹ (RNO 2001). All samples were gathered at a depth of 10 m by hand to minimize disturbance to the alga’s rhizosphere. At each site, approximately equal volumes of sediment (3,000–4,000 cm³) and associated C. taxifolia tissue were collected from three locations, separated by distances of at least 5 m to avoid sampling sediments linked by the same algal stolons (maximum stolon length = 2.8 m; see Meinesz et al. 1995). Uncolonized sediments were sampled in the same manner. Sediments were sampled from the sediment horizon to a depth of 10–15 cm. The samples were transported in plastic containers to the laboratory in Monaco and transferred into four 60-L flow-through aquaria within 3 h of collection. Two of the four aquaria were used to cultivate samples from each collection site on a 10–15-cm-deep basal layer of Fig. 1. Black zone in sediments surrounding the rhizoids of Caulerpa taxifolia caused by bacterial reduction of sulfate to sulfide. Fig. 2. Sample collection sites: (1) a dead bed of the sea grass Posidonia oceanica; (2) adjacent to the Monaco wastewater pre-treatment (A) and main (B) sewer outlets, whose locations are indicated by broken arrows. their original substratum. Each aquarium thus comprised sediments taken from each of the three intrasite locations, half of which bore cover of C. taxifolia and half of which did not. By maintaining colonized and uncolonized sediments in the same aquarium, it was possible to eliminate extraneous environmental variables and focus upon differences caused by the presence or absence of C. taxifolia, except, that is, for differences among the sediment and algal samples themselves. The other two aquaria were used to cultivate free-living C. taxifolia samples from each collection site in the absence of any basal substratum, after their rhizoids had been thoroughly cleaned of adhering sediment. All of the aquaria were fed continuously with fresh, filtered (2.5 \( \mu \)m) seawater, pumped to the laboratory from a depth of 50 m in the Mediterranean and heated to 22 \( \pm \) 0.5\( ^\circ \)C using thermostatically controlled immersion elements (1,000 W). Samples were grown under 100 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\) of white fluorescent light (6,000 K color temperature) on a 14:10 light:dark photoperiod for 4 weeks prior to experiments and then for the 4 weeks that it took to perform the acetylene reduction assays. Incubations to determine rates of acetylene reduction were carried out in wide-mouthed, clear glass jars placed on an agitating tray in a thermostatically controlled water bath. The bath was adjusted to the cultivation temperature. Each jar had an internal volume of 600 ml and possessed a clip-down, airtight lid. A 10-mm-diameter hole was cut in the lid and plugged with a rubber septum. The septum was positioned at the periphery of each lid to minimize shading of the samples. Algae, sediment, and algal–sediment associations were placed in the jars according to designated treatments, and volumes of seawater were added to leave gas headspace volumes of 250 ml. Blanks were prepared that contained seawater only. Purified acetylene was injected through the rubber septa using sterile syringes fitted with 0.6-mm-diameter needles to make up 20% of the gas phase (see Capone 1993). Samples were incubated for 4 h under 75 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\) of artificial daylight supplied by a 400-W overhead metal halide lamp. The reduced irradiance relative to the preassay conditions (100 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\)) was enforced by space constraints in the culture cabinet in which incubations were performed. That is, a smaller lamp needed to be fitted, which could deliver a maximum of 75 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\) when arranged to provide even illumination over the experimental subjects. Although 75 \( \mu \)mol m\(^{-2}\) s\(^{-1}\) is generally less than samples receive at a depth of 10 m, it is closer to the average irradiance received by the species over its depth range in the northern Mediterranean (near surface to 99 m; see Belsher and Meinesz 1995). During incubations, 550–600-\( \mu \)l samples of headspace gas were withdrawn from each jar using disposable syringes after 0, 15, 30, 60, 120, 180, and 210 or 240 min. Gas samples were stored until the end of each set of incubations by pushing the syringe needles into rubber bungs.
